=== PAGE 1 ===
*Australian Journal of Ecology* (1988) **13**, 505-518

# Demography of woody plants in relation to fire: *Banksia ericifolia* **L.f. and** *Petrophile pulchella* **(Schrad) R.Br.**

R. A. BRADSTOCK\*

*School of Biological Sciences. Macleay Building A12, University of Sydney, Sydney, NSW 2006, Australia*

M. A. O'CONNELL

*NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia*

#### **Abstract**

*Plants of* Banksia ericifolia *and* Petrophile pulchella *are sensitive to fire. Changes in population size under different fire regimes were estimated, based on measurements of post-fire seedling emergence, seedling survival, survival and seed production in established plants of differing ages, survival of seeds held in serotinous cones and seed-release in the periods between fire.*

*Seeds were first available at 5 years in* P. pulchella *and 6 years in* B. ericifolia. *Exact replacement would be possible when burnt at these ages, if seedling establishment were very high. Low establishment would delay replacement to 13 years of age in both species. Late summer/autumn fires of high intensity favour high establishment. Such fires at 8-10 year intervals would be tolerated without any sustained decline in numbers. Fires at 10-15 year intervals could occur regardless of season or intensity with little risk of a population decline. Large increases in numbers and density would follow fires spaced at 15-30 years. Enough seeds would be available for replacement up to about 50 years in both species. Viable seed-release in unburnt conditions was sufficient to compensate for deaths in stands over 20 years old, even with very low levels of establishment.*

*Two variables accounted for the biggest changes in numbers and density between generations interspersed by fires; namely the age at which a stand is burned and the proportion of seeds which emerge as seedlings. A comparison with other similar species showed similarities in controls on emergence and establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods and life spans.*

#### **Introduction**

Plants which rely on seeds for regeneration after fire (obligate seeders) form a prominent part of the vegetation in many fire-prone regions of the world (Gill 1981; Keeley 1981). Some obligate seeders are serotinous as their seeds are retained in the canopy and released by fire (Lotan 1976).

The present report presents demographic studies of two species which co-occur in fire-prone vegetation in the Sydney Region of south-eastern Australia; *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. and *Petrophile pulchella* (Schrad) R.Br. These perennial woody shrubs are frequently dominant in shrublands or the understorey of woodlands. Plants of both species are usually killed by fires of most intensities. Seeds (achenes in *P. pulchella)* are stored in woody infructescences, referred to here as cones, within closed follicles *(B. ericifolia)* or bracts *(P. pulchella).* Many other species of shrubs or small trees in these local vegetation types are also serotinous obligate seeders (Beadle 1940; Clemens & Franklin 1981; Benson 1985).

Crucial aspects of the demography of serotinous, obligate seeders are: (i) the time taken to first reproduction (primary juvenile period, Gill 1975) which determines the minimum possible interval at which fire may recur without causing extinction (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986) because seeds are usually non-dormant; (ii) seedling establishment post-fire, which is determined by rainfall, tempera-

\*Present address: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, Box N189 Grosvenor St, Sydney, NSW 2000, Australia.
=== PAGE 2 ===
506 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

ture, predators and the rate of release of seeds which, in turn, may be influenced by the season and intensity of fire (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bond *et al.* 1984; Cowling & Lamont 1984, 1985; McMahon 1984); (iii) the size of the pre-fire seed-bank, which is dependent on current storage plus new seeds added after each episode of seasonal fruiting minus losses of stored seeds in existing fruits (McMaster & Zedler 1981; Bond 1984; Gill & McMahon 1986); (iv) rates of survival of seedlings, juveniles and adults; (v) any subsequent establishment in unburnt conditions. Survival will be partly determined by density and age (Schlesinger & Gill 1978; Morris & Myerscough 1983, 1988). If establishment is absent in such conditions, the numbers and density in an even-aged post-fire generation will decline to low levels as the time since last fire nears the limit of longevity of the species (Specht *et al.* 1958; Ashton 1976; Gill & McMahon 1986).

These factors can be linked in a demographic model to predict population size over successive generations subject to re-occurring fires. Such information would provide a detailed basis for the management of fire-prone plant communities. However, few studies have attempted to relate changes in population size to fire regimes (Zedler 1977; Kruger 1983). At present there is much pressure for repeated burning of the vegetation containing the study species at intervals of less than 10 years for the purpose of fuel reduction. Often such prescribed fires are ignited in the cool months, between April and October. If informed fire-management is to take place it is important to know how these fire regimes and their alternatives may affect these potentially vulnerable, serotinous, obligate seeders. This study aimed to answer the following questions.

(1) What is the shortest interval between fires (maximum fire frequency) that either species can withstand for a sustained period (e.g. about 100 years) without suffering a prolonged decrease in population size?

(2) How is this maximum tolerable fire frequency affected by differences in the amounts of seedling emergence and survival occurring after different fires?

(3) Are variations in seedling emergence and survival related to the seasonal timing and intensity of fires?

(4) What are the likely trends in numbers and density of stands when fires occur infrequently?

(5) How do these species compare with other serotinous obligate seeders?

#### **Methods**

#### *Study sites*

The survival of plants more than 3 years of age, and the sizes of their seed-banks, were studied in seven areas situated within the Brisbane Water National Park, approximately 50 km north of Sydney, from 1980-83. These areas were last burned in 1977, 1976, 1975, 1974, 1973, 1968 and 1960 respectively, determined from fire-history maps and aerial photographs. All were located on ridge-tops of sandy earths derived from Hawkesbury Sandstone. Distance from the coast varied between 3 and 15 km.

Observations on the emergence and survival of seedlings (<3 years of age) were made in populations after four unplanned fires and in one experiment, between December 1980 and November 1982. These were located in the same area and had similar site characteristics to those populations used for the study of established plants.

#### *Seedling emergence and survival*

The number of seedlings that emerged after each fire was counted in 40-70 quadrats (0.1 m<sup>2</sup>) for each species. The number of pre-fire seeds on dead plants was estimated by counting the number of cones held on branches in transects adjacent to the study quadrats, after the fire. The number of seeds per cone and the proportion of stored seeds that were intact and viable were estimated in cones taken from nearby unburnt stands. These procedures are described below.

The fate of the seedlings was followed until mid 1983. Two alternative models of survival, the exponential and power function (Silvertown 1982) were fitted. No model is given for Burn IV in *P. pulchella* due to the small numbers of plants which emerged. Indeed, models were fitted only when data for major cohorts of 10 or more seedlings were available.
=== PAGE 3 ===
*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 507

Emergence was studied in two experiments (commenced May and November 1982) in which artificial ashbeds were prepared and known quantities of seeds sown. Quadrats (1 m × 1 m) were prepared by removing all plant cover and litter. Heat was applied to the exposed soil using propane burners. Harvested plant material and litter were ashed and placed on the soil after the heating had ceased. Either 50 (May 1982) or 100 (November 1982) seeds of each species were scattered on the quadrats several days later. The number of emerged seedlings was counted on average every month for a year after the starting dates.

#### *Survival in established plants*

Survival was measured in samples of 50 or more plants of both species which were tagged in late 1980-early 1981. Each sample was located within quadrats (1.0 m × 1.0 m or 0.5 m × 0.5 m) on two adjacent lines randomly situated on a 20 m baseline located in thick patches of either species. All tagged plants were assumed to have arisen as seedlings after the previous fire in each area. The initial height of each plant was recorded.

Plants of *B. ericifolia* in some areas (burned 1977, 1974) were located solely on shallow soils (depth 0.3-0.4 m) and these were stunted in height and spindly in form compared with populations located on deep soils (depth 1.0-1.5 m; burned 1973, 1968, 1960). One area (burned 1975) contained plants on both soils. One sample was tagged in each area on each available soil type. A second was then established in each of the 1968 and 1960 areas, several hundred metres from the first.

Plants of *P. pulchella* were not as common on shallow soils, therefore samples were tagged only on deep soils. These were separate but often close to the *B. ericifolia* samples. No sampling was done in the 1976 or 1973 areas. Two samples were tagged in each of the other areas. A fire in 1982 destroyed a single sample of each species in the 1960 area.

Plants were checked twice yearly from the beginning of 1981 until October 1983 and the proportion of deaths was measured for each area to test for differences in mortality between soils in *B. ericifolia* and between populations of differing age in both species using G tests of independence.

#### *Seed-survival*

Ten cones from each of four age classes (1, 5, 9 and 15 years) were harvested from each sample in 1983. These harvests were spread over three to four plants. Ages were estimated either by direct observation (1 and 5 years only) or by position and appearance (9 and 15 years). Cones of 9 and 15 years were those borne nearest the base of plants and presumed to be from the earliest cohort set in the 1968 stand and from the third oldest cohort in the 1960 stand. The latter origin was assumed because some cones in a more advanced state of degradation were found on the ground and these were assumed to be slightly older. In areas where only a single sample was available for each soil type a replicate of ten cones was harvested 50-100 m from the tagged plants. Two samples of cones were also taken from *P. pulchella* plants at the same time as sampling from *B. ericifolia* in the 1973 area.

Counts were made, in the laboratory, of total follicles or bracts and the number that was open and empty was recorded. Cones of *B. ericifolia* were heated in an oven at 200°C for 10 min to open follicles and aid seed removal. This treatment had no effect on seed viability (Bradstock 1985). Cones of *P. pulchella* were left unheated for several weeks after which seed extraction was possible.

Twenty unopened follicles/bracts were selected randomly and examined and the seeds within were scored as damaged by predators or intact. If intact, seeds were classified as filled, desiccated or aborted. Viability of intact, filled seeds was determined in batches of 50 by germination on filter paper in petri dishes maintained at saturation for 2-3 months. Germination occurred under optimum conditions (12:12 h day:night cycle of 15:5°C; Bradstock 1985) in an environmental cabinet.

The relationship between the proportion of seeds per cone surviving (i.e. intact, filled, viable, unreleased seeds) and age was described using various linear and non-linear models. The preferred model was chosen via a comparison of the percentage variances (PV) accounted for. These PV were the differences between the residual and total mean squares expressed as a percentage of the total mean square.
=== PAGE 4 ===
508 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

#### *Seed-bank estimation*

All new cones set in the samples during the study were counted. Cone production during 1984-85 in the 1960 stands was also measured. Collections of 10 cones produced in two flowering seasons between 1981 and 1983 were made from each sample to determine seed-set per cone. A further 10 cones were harvested in areas with only one sample per soil-depth tested. Mean total annual seed production per plant was thus calculated and then described as a function of age by various linear and nonlinear models from which a preferred model was chosen by a comparison of PV.

Seed-bank at any given age (per plant) was predicted by estimating the number of seeds (one seed per follicle or bract) set in each of the successive annual cohorts produced up to that age, using the preferred seed production model. In each cohort survival was then calculated using the preferred survival model for each species. The numbers of surviving seeds from each cohort at a given age were then summed to give an estimate of total stored viable seeds for that age. This was repeated for all ages between the time of first reproduction and 40 years. The estimates above 25 years were therefore extrapolations beyond the age limit of the samples. Allowance was made for the time between flowering and fruit maturity which is about one year in both species.

A further, alternative estimate of seed-bank was made. Seed production was stopped at age 30 years and the attrition of existing seeds was predicted up to an age of 100 years.

#### *Seed-release between fires*

The mean number of viable seeds released annually (per plant) in each sample in unburnt conditions was estimated. Samples of cones of four different ages were marked in the 1968 and 1960 samples in mid 1981. Two age classes of cones (1 and 5 years in 1981, method of ageing similar to that described above) were marked in all other samples. The oldest cones in each sample were also marked and in 1981 these were estimated to be 7 and 13 years old. Follicles (*B. ericifolia*) or bracts (*P. pulchella*) which were open and empty were marked. Cones were rechecked after 2 years and the number of follicles/bracts was counted along with those which had opened and shed seeds. Rates of seed-release were compared between samples and cone ages using analysis of variance.

All cones set before 1981 were counted in each sample. The mean number of seeds released per plant was then estimated from the product of the measured annual rate of release per cone age class and the mean number of cones in each class. Cones set before 1981 were allocated to the nearest age class and a correction was made for viability.

#### *The effect of frequent fires*

The effect of three successive fires, separated by intervals of identical length, on the number of plants in a hypothetical stand of each species was estimated. Plants living in the first interval were called first generation and in the second, second generation. The first generation immediate pre-fire number was set at 50 and model stands were assumed to be similar to the sample stands in other respects, such as density. Eleven calculations were done, using values between 5 and 15 years for the 'between-fire' interval.

Second generation stand size (*N*) was calculated as a function of the interval (*i*) between fires using:

*N* = *B* × *E* × *Ss* × *Se* (1)

where *B* = first generation seed-bank size, *E* = proportion of seeds emerging as post-fire seedlings, *Ss* = proportion of seedlings which survive and *Se* = proportion of living plants > 3 years old at *i* years of age. Values of *N* were divided by 50 to give estimates of proportional change in numbers. These estimates were plotted against size of gap between fires. Opposing, extreme values of *E* and *Ss* were used to produce high and low estimates of proportional change.

#### **Results**

#### *Seedling emergence and survival*

In both species, emergence was spread over periods of up to 9 months after the fires or experiments. The number, density and proportion of seedlings that emerged from seeds were variable (Table 1). Pulses of emergence pro-
=== PAGE 5 ===
*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 509

duced cohorts with differing birth dates in each natural fire. In *B. ericifolia* the power and exponential models were found to be the models of best fit (Table 2) while in *P. pulchella* the power function was the model of best fit (Table 2). In some cases neither model fitted the data well (Table 2).

#### *Seed-bank estimation*

Substantial differences occurred between years and samples, in both the numbers of cones produced and the seeds set within them. These produced large variations in seed production (Fig. 4). There was no evidence of any serial correlation between data from successive years for individual samples.

In *P. pulchella,* seed-production was very high in the 1960 sample (Fig. 4). Most cones were young which indicated that cone-production may accelerate rapidly between the ages of 15 and 20 years.

The alternative values of E were set at 0.5 and 0.05. These bounded the range observed in the field (Table 1). #### **Discussion**

#### *Effects of frequent fires*

The importance of emergence and survival was reffected in the variability of the interval between fires at which stand replacement would be possible (Fig. 7). Burning at an interval close to 13 years could be done with little regard to other factors such as season or intensity of fire without risk of a decline in numbers. The low levels of emergence and survival (Tables 1,2) used to produce this estimate were the product of a severe drought in the area (Bureau of Meteorology, pers. comm.). It is likely that fires in most years will produce at least a similar or larger number of seedlings. Survival of established plants may also be higher, for this reason.

Fire-managers may wish to burn as often as twice a decade, hence it is necessary to know the limit to which fire frequency can be reduced below 13 years without risking a serious decline in numbers. Seasons and intensities of fire may become important in such

*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 513

circumstances as will year to year variability in rainfall.

Bradstock (1985) found that emergence in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* varied with rainfall, soil moisture and temperature. High summer temperatures impose a form of exogenous dormancy on seeds (definition of Mott & Groves 1981), restricting emergence to the cooler months. Seeds which lie on the soil over summer lose some viability. The amount of emergence was positively correlated with the period of time the soil surface (0-1.0 cm) remains at field capacity after rain. Seed predation was minimal in burnt areas.

Rainfall near the coast in the Sydney Region is highest, on average, from January to July (100-130 mm/month), and lowest from August to December (70-80 mm/month); however, there is great year to year variation.

FIG. 5. Mean number of stored viable seeds (seed-bank) per plant, under two regimes of seed production: continuous (——), ceased at 30 years (- - -).

When evaporation is taken into account, the average period of sustained high soil moisture is May-July (early winter). Emergence may therefore be highest after fires which are timed so that most seeds are released in early winter. Seed-release will be most rapid after high intensity fires (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981; Bradstock 1985) and such fires in late summer-autumn will cause most seeds to be released by early winter. In contrast, low inten-

514 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

sity fires at this time will prolong seed-release over winter and spring. Late summer-autumn, high intensity fires will therefore, on average, yield optimum emergence. A similar fire regime giving optimum emergence in other species of serotinous Proteaceae has been observed by Specht *et al.* (1958), Specht (1981), Bond *et al.* (1984), Cowling and Lamont (1984a, 1984b, 1985), McMahon (1984). Mechanisms in each case were generally similar to those described here.

While mortality of plants older than 100 days was due mainly to drought, younger seedlings died during both short dry spells and heavy rain (Bradstock 1985) when they were broken by raindrop impact or washed away. Bradstock (1985) concluded that the risk of death at the most vulnerable age (< 100 days; Table 2) would be minimized when seedlings emerged in early winter. This reinforced the conclusion that late summer fires are optimal in producing seedlings.

After successive fires at 8 years, the proportional change in second generation stand size may vary from 9.8 to 0.5 in *B. ericifolia* and from 7.2 to 0.6 in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 7). The daily rainfall patterns for Sydney over 50 years (Bureau of Meterology, pers. comm.) show that a winter containing two successive months of low soil surface moisture occurs on average once every decade whereas very wet winters in which the soil is more or less continually moist occur several times a decade (Bradstock 1985). Thus fires of optimal season and intensity occurring 8 years apart would be followed by a dry winter and a subsequent decline in post-fire numbers, once every 80-100 years. More usually these fires would be followed by wet winters which would permit an increase in numbers. Hence an optimal regime in terms of season and intensity with an 8-10 year interval may cause fluctuations in numbers but is unlikely to send either species into a persistent decline if sustained over a period of up to 100 years. A 6-8 year cycle would be hazardous, due to a lower seed-bank and the increased probability of encountering dry post-fire conditions.

Reproduction is delayed in *B. ericifolia* growing on shallow soils and such stands may decline when fires occur less than 15 years apart. Observations indicate that the primary juvenile period may extend to more than 8 years and also that the seed-bank size may be less than on deep soils.

There are, therefore, two consecutive phases in which plants are susceptible to recurrent fires: first, during the primary juvenile period and second, the subsequent time up to the age at which exact self-replacement of stands is possible. So far most attention has been given to describing the lengths of primary juvenile periods. Values given here fell within the ranges already reported for these species (Benson 1985) and for other serotinous obligate seeders of the Proteaceae (3-11 years; Kruger 1983; Lamont 1985). Measurements of this second critical phase need to be made if serotinous obligate seeders are to be used as indicator species in fire-prone vegetation. It
=== PAGE 11 ===
*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 515

may be useful if correlations exist between this and other demographic characteristics, particularly the length of the primary juvenile period. For example, is first reproduction at an early age always followed by a short interval to the age of self-replacement or vice versa?

Replacement ages for the study species were similar, despite differences in seedling-survival, early rates of development of seed-bank and primary juvenile period. Gill and McMahon (1986) reported that in *Banksia ornata*, a serotinous obligate seeder, common in parts of southern Australia, stand replacement may be likely after 16 years of age if post-fire emergence took place from 20% of available seeds. Seeds first become available at about 6 years in *B. ornata* (Gill & McMahon 1986), a figure comparable to that in *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella.* Despite this similarity, populations of *B. ornata* may decline under some repeated cycles of fire less than 15 years apart, whilst *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella* populations may increase or remain stable. This difference was primarily due to a slower rate of accumulation of seed-bank in *B. ornata*, though other possible differences in projected survival rate were also present. Similarly, Kruger and Bigalke (1984) reported that in *Protea repens,* a shrub of the South African fynbos, the primary juvenile period may be 4-5 years (ripe seeds first available), but replacement age may be 10-12 years. It is most prudent to conclude that there is little current evidence of any consistent linkage between these key events. Further demographic studies amongst a wider range of species are needed to confirm this.

#### *Effects of infrequent fires*

The present study was hampered by a lack of old populations (>25 years). This prevented direct measurements of life span and seed-production in very old plants. It was necessary to extrapolate trends from younger populations and anecdotal evidence to describe what happens when fire is excluded for long periods.

In the seed-bank models (Fig. 5) seed-production was arbitrarily set to cease at 30 years. However, Bradstock and Myerscough (1981) observed the occurrence of stands of *B. ericifolia* older than this (these also contained *P. pulchella*) in which seeds were still being produced. The modeled storages will therefore underestimate the trend in real stands. Nevertheless, these suggested that enough seeds would be available for replacement for up to about 45 years in *B. ericifolia* and 90 years in *P. pulchella.* The life spans of these species are more likely to be less than 50 years (Bradstock & Myerscough 1981), hence in reality, senescence will hasten the decline of the seed-bank through the death of plants and replacement ages may be much nearer 30 years. The fall of viable seeds onto the litter and soil will increase as a consequence and, if seed-production occurs beyond 30 years, this pool of released seeds will be very large. If these assumptions are correct, changes in number and seed-bank may be quite similar in their pattern to those described by Gill and McMahon 1986 for *B. ornata.* Kruger and Bigalke (1984) also reported a similar decline in numbers after 30 years in some serotinous obligate seeders from South African shrublands, and suggested that life spans for dominant species of this kind fell within the range 20-50 years.

In samples that are more than 20 years of age the number of viable seeds released each year (Fig. 6) greatly exceeded the number of plants that died annually (Figs 1, 2). Bradstock (1985) found that the heavy cover of plants and seedling predators restricted establishment from this pool of available seeds. However, a few seedlings are likely to survive in both species. A rough calculation can be done to estimate the number which may establish in a stand of 50 plants. Average conditions of soil moisture in any year will usually be adequate to give 10% emergence of available seeds. If 5% of these survive for 3 years (about eight times lower survival than in burnt conditions; Table 2), then 21-24 year old stands would produce two (*B. ericifolia*) and 12 (*P. pulchella*) seedlings annually. Such recruits would join the ranks of small suppressed plants which are subject to high mortality and would probably have little chance of reproducing (Bradstock 1985).

At greater ages, when seed-release and mortality may be high, gaps in the canopy caused by senescence of dominants may appear. Seedling predators may become satiated as a result (e.g. Bond 1984a; O'Dowd & Gill 1984) and these conditions may promote the emergence, growth and reproduction of new plants. The relative abilities of *B. ericifolia, P. pulchella*
=== PAGE 12 ===
516 *R. A. Bradstock and M. A. O'Connell*

and other species to exploit gaps and openings may determine whether self-perpetuation in large numbers is possible in the absence of fire. More work is needed to determine regeneration processes in older stands and their scarcity means that some effort needs to be made to preserve unburnt areas in the future.

Fires, 20-30 years apart, will create very high density stands and the absence of these in the study area may be due to a history of burning at a higher frequency.

#### *Effects of density*

Fire regimes may be used to increase or decrease the density of stands. For instance, if the relationships in Figs 1-7 hold true for much of the potential range of densities, then it may be possible, for example, to thin very dense stands and then hold them in this state. Several adverse fire-cycles (e.g. low intensity spring fires, less than 10 years apart) followed by a 10 year cycle of high intensity autumn fires would achieve this result.

The density of a stand will change with age as plants die and the chronosequence in Table 3 may indicate the approximate trend. Bradstock (1985) found that density had no effect on the survival of seedlings older than 100 days. There were also no obvious effects of density on survival at older ages in either species, including the 1975 samples in *P. pulchella* (Fig. 2; Table 3), although dead plants tended to be small suppressed individuals in both species. Morris and Myerscough (1983, 1988) found evidence for density-dependent mortality in *B. ericifolia* stands of very high density (initial sample: 140 plants m<sup>-2</sup>) between the ages of 4 and 9 years.

In both *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella,* the proportion of plants that continues to produce cones declined with age (Bradstock 1985) so that over time the increase in reproductive effort (Fig. 4) came from a small number of dominant individuals (Bradstock 1985). This pattern of reproduction amongst individuals may affect the relationship between density and seed-bank if the survival of dominant reproductive plants is unaffected by the number of suppressed individuals. The number of plants which reproduce and the amount of seeds produced may then be fixed above a moderate threshold of density, as indicated by experimental studies in other single-species populations (Harper 1977; Silvertown 1982). Further evidence of Morris and Myerscough (1988) showed that *B. ericifolia* plants at densities of 27.5 plants m<sup>-2</sup> had set a mean of 345 ± 92 seeds m<sup>-2</sup> at 8 years whereas high density plants (142 m<sup>-2</sup>) produced 225 ± 80 seeds m<sup>-2</sup>. If seed-bank size is fixed across the upper range of densities then its prime determinant will be stand age. The perpetuation of very dense stands would then be possible only after longer fire-free intervals than those described here for lower density samples.

Density and numbers may also be influenced by pollinators. Paton and Turner (1985) found that introduced bees may double the numbers of seeds set in *B. ericifolia* cones. The introduction of exotic bees may therefore have caused a massive increase in density and numbers in stands containing this species without any concurrent change in fire frequency. Other changes in species composition may have followed.

#### **Conclusions**

All components of fire regime can influence a change in numbers and density, between generations, of *B. ericifolia* and *P. pulchella.* However, the largest change was due to differences in the age at which stands were burnt and the proportion of seeds which emerged as seedlings. Seasonal controls on seedling establishment, lengths of primary juvenile periods, effects of seed or seedling predators in unburnt conditions, and changes in structure of old stands and life spans, are generally similar in southern hemisphere species, particularly within the family, Proteaceae. However, demographic behaviour of fire-prone species cannot be predicted solely from any single characteristic such as survival, degree of serotiny (seed-survival in cones), seed-bank size or success of emergence. Any attempt to compare and classify species on their relative ability to withstand specific fire regimes, without a quantitative overview of the life-cycle, could be misleading.

There may be little reason to assume that if reproduction commences early, then enough seeds will also be available to ensure replacement at a relatively early age. Quantitative variations in all the important components of the
=== PAGE 13 ===
*Demography of woody plants in relation to fire* 517

life-cycle may exist within a species and correlations between these components and obvious site factors need to be studied (e.g. Cowling & Lamont 1985). Managers concerned with conserving populations at stable numbers should therefore use, as an indicator of the minimum interval between fires, the serotinous obligate seeder within their estate, that is slowest to reach self-replacement.

8	# **Population structure and reproductive status of two** *Banksia* **shrubs at various times after fire**
9	
10	Charles Zammit<sup>1</sup> & Mark Westoby\*
11	
12	*School of Biological Sciences, Macquarie University, North Ryde N.S.W. 2113, Australia* 
13	
14	<sup>1</sup>*Present address: Department of Biology, San Diego State University, San Diego CA 92182, USA* 
15	
16	Keywords: Australia, *Banksia,* Fire, Population structure, Regeneration strategy, Seed production, Serotiny
17	
18	# **Abstract**
19	
20	Populations of the obligate-seeder, *Banksia ericifolia,* were even-aged. Seedling recruitment occurred only after fire. Mean genet size (height + canopy diameter; H + D) increased progressively with elapsed time since fire in stands last burnt 2-23 years before 1981. Populations of a co-occurring resprouter, *B. oblongifolia,* were mixed-aged. Genet size varied significantly between stands, but this variation was not explained by regressions of H + D on years since fire. In addition *B. oblongifolia* seedlings were recruited both after fire and in patches of heath unburnt for 16 years.
21	
22	Most flower and seed production in *B. oblongifolia* occurred in the stands last burnt less than 10 years previously. More than 30% of genets had not produced cones since the last fire, irrespective of how many years had elapsed. In contrast, few *B. ericifolia* genets had produced cones five years after fire, but by 16 years after fire nearly 100% had. Overall, about 51% of *B. ericifolia* inflorescences and about 28% of *B. oblongifolia* inflorescences set seed. The number of seeds in seed-bearing cones was not significantly different between species.
23	
24	Resprouting *B. oblongifolia* genets began flowering sooner after fire, but *B. ericifolia* subsequently overtook them in accumulating a bank of serotinous seeds. In the stand unburnt for 23 years the largest *B. ericifolia* genets had more than twice as many cones as the largest co-occurring *B. oblongifolia.* However, when accumulated cone production was compared for genets of equal H + D over all stands, there was no difference between species.
25	
26	#### **Introduction**
27	
28	There have been two general approaches to ecological studies of fire effects on vegetation. Community ecologists have monitored regeneration of species assemblages after single fires in Australia (Hill & Read, 1984; Purdie & Slatyer, 1976; Siddiqi *et al.,* 1976; Specht *et al.,* 1958), or studied floristic changes by sampling from communities of known ages (Bell & Koch, 1980; Russell & Parsons, 1978). On the other hand population biologists have examined the effects of fire on population structure (Ashton, 1976; Griffin & Friedel, 1984), seedling recruitment (Bradstock & Myerscough, 1981; Scalan & O'Rourke, 1982) and flowering (Gill & Ingwersen, 1976; Pyke, 1983). A recent volume summarises these and other aspects of the nature, impact and management of fires in the Australian biota (Gill *et al.,* 1981).
29	
30	<sup>\*</sup> We thank the New South Wales National Parks & Wildlife Service for permission to do this work in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park. We are grateful to Don Adamson, Lynn Day, David Haig and James Sim for constructive comments on earlier drafts.
31	=== PAGE 2 ===
32	12
33	
34	Here we compare the population characteristics, in relation to time elapsed since fire, of two co-occurring *Banksia* (Proteaceae) shrub species common in the fire-prone scrublands of the Sydney Basin. *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. is an obligate-seeder. Individuals (genets) are killed by fire and so depend entirely on successfully recruiting seedlings for the persistence of lineages. Genets are single stemmed and can be up to 5 m tall. Ericoid leaves are arranged in a roughly spherical, continuous canopy, which covers up to 8 m<sup>2</sup> at maturity. In contrast, *B. oblongifolia* Cav. resprouts from a lignotuber after fire. In this species there are two levels of demographic response to fire: the mortality and recruitment of genets (lignotubers) and the mortality and recruitment of ramets (resprouting stems) on each genet. Individual shrubs seldom grow taller than 2 m in the heathlands of the Sydney Basin. However their canopies, made up of discontinuous clusters of large serrate leaves, may span up to 5 m<sup>2</sup>. Both of these *Banksia* shrubs produce a variable number of persistent flowering spikes annually, each of which supports 500-2500+ flowers. A single winged seed is stored in each woody follicle, and follicles are clustered along the flowering spike to form a seed-bearing cone retained in the canopy. Seed release occurs mainly after fire ruptures the follicle, a trait known as serotiny.
35	
36	Our aim in this comparative survey was to investigate how size frequency distributions and reproductive activity changed during the interval between fires in the two species. By choosing two species which are closely related but differ in the fundamental fire-response characteristic of resprouting vs obligate-seeding, we hoped to develop hypotheses about how other aspects of life history are associated with these characteristics.
37	
38	#### **Study area and methods**
39	
40	All surveys were done during March-August 1981 in the Lambert Peninsula region of Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (33°55'S, 151°10'E), about 40 km north of Sydney, Australia. This landscape is part of the Hornsby Plateau, a mid-Triassic formation made up of eroded quartz sandstones interspersed with shales: it supports a number of vegetation types (Thomas & Benson, 1985). Shallow soils, some with impeded drainage, support the heath and scrub (sensu Specht, 1981) common on the plateaus of the peninsula. *Banksia ericifolia* and *B. oblongifolia* are common in the heath, scrub and some woodlands of this region (Thomas & Benson, 1985) and they also co-occur in other sandstone scrublands in the Sydney Basin (Siddiqi *et al.,* 1972).
41	
42	Fire history records (New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service; Northern Metropolitan Office) were used to compile maps of all fire boundaries recorded within the Lambert Peninsula (about 70 km<sup>2</sup>) between 1943-1980. All areas burnt between 1943 and 1957 had been burnt at least once again after 1958. The oldest scrub stand had been unburnt for 23 years. Areas which were last burnt in 1958, 1965, 1973, 1975 and 1979 were selected to represent a time-since-fire sequence. Their boundaries were validated against aerial photographs taken within a few years of the fires (New South Wales Lands Dept. Cumberland series; 1956, 1960, 1970, 1978). This comparison confirmed the overall reliability of the fire records, but highlighted the patchy nature of some fires. The sizes of suitable study areas varied widely. The 1973 and 1975 fires were confined, and only a small portion of the area burnt in 1958 had not been burnt again. The 1965 and 1979 fires burnt through large areas of the park and substantial areas had not been burnt again. Stands which supported both *B. ericifolia* and *B. oblongifolia* and which were similar in topography and vegetation structure were selected as survey sites (Table 1). We chose stands which were on ridgetops or north facing upper slopes. We avoided areas of excessive exposed rock: most transects had less than 10% exposed rock. We generally avoided stands which supported trees, however scattered trees were present in some restricted sites.
43	
44	Up to five 30 m transects were randomly positioned in each of these sites. Along each transect we examined all plants rooted within 2 m on either side. We recorded height, two maximum canopy diameters, the number of current (1981) inflorescences, the number of seed-bearing cones and the number of barren, old inflorescence spikes. *Banksia ericifolia* at the site last burnt in 1979 were more abundant, and transects 1 m wide were examined. Current inflorescences were always intact. We found no evidence of destruction by insectivorous birds, as reported by Scott & Black (1981) and McFarland (1985).
45	
46	We could distinguish entire lignotubers for most *B. oblongifolia* genets. However, when this proved difficult because parts of the lignotuber were buried, or when large lignotubers had rotted out in part, we probed the lignotuber perimeter with a metal spike. It is possible that on a few occasions we incorrectly classified several smaller, separate lignotubers as a single larger lignotuber. We counted the number of attached live and dead ramets on each genet.
47	
48	We calculated several measures of the size of plants, using

69	
70	canopy height, mean canopy diameter, lignotuber area and stem basal area in various combinations. These were all highly intercorrelated (Zammit, 1986). Here we use height plus mean diameter *(H+D)* as a size measure, having found no evidence that other measures were more meaningful. In other perennial species *H+D* is well correlated with plant age and stem diameter (Crisp & Lange, 1976), and with above ground biomass (Grice, 1984). We also harvested seed-bearing cones from nearby individuals of both species and compared their lengths and seed numbers.
71	
72	In this survey we followed many other workers by examining populations which had been burnt at different times in the past, and interpreting these results as indicating how one population would behave over time. It is desirable to make explicit the reasoning involved. Strictly, our statistics only test for significant differences between different stands created in different fire-years. Because of the restricted area available for some fire-years, we did not study replicate sites within each fire-year. However, even if we had studied replicate sites for each fire, the difficulty would not have been removed, because the sites burnt in any given year are likely to be a very nonrandom sample from all sites. The problem cannot be solved by means of statistics. It is unavoidably a matter of interpretation whether effects are due to differences between site locations, or to differences in time elapsed since fire. Our approach has been to analyse the results in relation to time since fire, and to regard time elapsed as the likely cause when it seems improbable that such a pattern could arise accidentally from differences among site locations. It should be noted that since both species were sampled at the same sites, differences between species cannot be attributed to between-site effects.
73	
74	#### **Results**
75	
76	#### *Genet size and reproductive status*
77	
78	Seed-bearing *B. ericifolia* cones were significantly longer than *B. oblongifolia* (12.2±3.8 cm vs 10.2±2.6 cm, *F*<sub>1,29</sub> = 7.03, *p* < 0.001), however, there was no difference in seed number per cone (*B. ericifolia* 42±20; *B. oblongifolia* 39±16, *F*<sub>1,29</sub> = 0.5, ns). A direct count of the number of seed-bearing cones per genet therefore provided a nondestructive and comparative index of the number of seeds stored in serotinous cones.
79	
80	In *B. ericifolia* differences among stands in mean H + D, mean cones accumulated, and mean seed-bearing cones accumulated were well described by linear regressions on years since fire (Figs. 1a, b, c). The distribution of *B. ericifolia* H + D size classes between stands followed the expected pattern for the obligate seeding strategy; a single cohort of seedlings was recruited after fire and a new population of genets established (Fig. 2). Sizes of the members of a cohort were normally distributed, but there was wider variance as populations thinned and reached reproductive maturity (Fig. 2). These patterns support the view that populations of the obligate-seeder, *B. ericifolia,* are even-aged.
81	
82	Mean H + D for *B. oblongifolia* genets did not increase consistently with time since fire. However stands had different frequency distributions of *H+D* (Fig. 2) and different means (Fig. 1a), which may be due to different long term fire histories of particular sites. On the other hand mean cones accumulated and mean seed-bearing cones accumu-

(a) Mean H + D of *B. ericifolia* (●) genets increased significantly (H + D = 29.33 + 19.19 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.88, p < 0.001). The sizes of *B. oblongifolia* (○) genets were not influenced by the elapsed time since fire (r<sup>2</sup> = 0.06, ns). (b) Mean cones accumulated (TCP) increased significantly in both species (*B. ericifolia:* TCP = -6.22 + 1.46 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.90, p < 0.013; *B. oblongifolia:* TCP = 2.29 + 0.63 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.96, p < 0.003). (c) Mean seed-bearing cones accumulated (RS) increased significantly in both species (*B. ericifolia:* RS = -4.59 + 0.70 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.98, p < 0.018; *B. oblongifolia:* RS = 0.09 + 0.21 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.99, p < 0.004). (d) The proportion of TCP which produced seed-bearing cones (%RS) declined significantly in *B. ericifolia* (%RS = 69.6 - 1.2 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.90, p < 0.02), and did not vary over time in *B. oblongifolia* (r<sup>2</sup> = 0.31, ns).

89	
90	#### *Genet density*
91	
92	The density of *B. oblongifolia* genets did not vary systematically with increasing time since fire. Some transects from the 1965 stand, however, supported about twice as many genets as those from all other transects (Fig. 3). Most of these were from the smallest size class (Fig. 2). In contrast, the density of *B. ericifolia* genets was higher in the 1979 stand (2 years after fire) than in the rest.
93	
94	#### *Influence of time since fire on reproductive status*
95	
96	Flowering response in 1981 was different between

Mean H+D was significantly different between stands for both species: for *B. ericifolia* X<sup>2</sup> = 38.3, for *B. oblongifolia* X<sup>2</sup> = 18.8, p < 0.001; analysis was by a mixed-model ANOVA which relaxed some requirements for balanced design and equality of variances. The test statistic is a maximum likelihood estimate of the variance components of the general mixed-model ANOVA (BMDP3V; Dixon *et al.,* 1983).

100	species from the same stand, and also between stands. Current *B. oblongifolia* inflorescences were most abundant in genets from the stand burnt in 1979, while current inflorescence abundance on *B. ericifolia* genets was highest in the stand burnt in 1958 (Table 2). The percentage of genets flowering in 1981, out of all genets which had flowered at some time since the last fire, is given in parentheses

117	
118	The proportion of genets which had flowered at some time in a stand was also different between species. About 70% of *B. oblongifolia* genets had flowered in the 1973 stand, while a smaller proportion had flowered in other stands irrespective of when they last burnt (Fig. 2). In contrast, the proportion of *B. ericifolia* genets which had flowered increased with increasing time since fire. About 90% of all plants in the 1973 stand had flowered, and in the 1958 stand all genets had produced inflorescences at some time (Fig. 2).
119	
120	Resprouting *B. oblongifolia* genets flowered sooner than *B. ericifolia,* but they added new cones more slowly thereafter. In the 1958 stand *B. ericifolia* genets, averaged over all individuals which had flowered, supported about 2.5 times as many cones as *B. oblongifolia* (Fig. 1b).
121	
122	Averaged over genets in all stands, a significantly lower percentage of cones bore seed in *B. oblongifolia* (28%) than in *B. ericifolia* (51%) (*F*<sub>1,449</sub> = 58.7, *p* < 0.001). Percentage of cones bearing seeds from *B. oblongifolia* genets did not differ between stands (Fig. 1d). Percentage of cones bearing seeds declined significantly in *B. ericifolia* with increasing time since fire (Fig. 1d). However this effect was not strong enough to offset *B. ericifolia's* increase in accumulated cone production with time since fire.
123	
124	Except for *B. ericifolia* in the stand last burnt in 1958, most genets of both *Banksia* species supported less than twenty cones in total. Only a few genets carried more than 10 seed-bearing cones (Fig. 4). Accumulated seed production over about 20 years for most genets therefore added up to less than 500 seeds.
125	
126	#### *Genet size and reproductive status*
127	
128	For many plant species size is a better predictor of ecological performance than age (White, 1980). Larger genets of both species were the first to support reproductive structures. As the even-aged populations of *B. ericifolia* matured all plants reached a reproductive size (Fig. 2). This was not the case in the *B. oblongifolia* populations, where even in a stand unburnt for 23 years the smallest genets had never been reproductive (Fig. 2). For both *Banksia* species mean accumulated cone production was strongly related to genet size in all stands, irrespective of time elapsed since fire (Fig. 5). Averaged over all stands, cone production was very similar between species for any given H + D (Fig. 5).
129	
130	There was no difference in the proportion of cones which bore seed between different sized ge-

Perhaps in older stands larger genets are more efficient at producing seeds, or more inflorescences in larger shrubs escape the damaging effects of predators (Zammit & Hood, 1986). Generally *B. ericifolia* cones were about twice as likely to bear seed, although this difference was less clear at the site last burnt in 1958 (Fig. 6).

148	#### *Influence of time since fire and genet size on populations of* B. oblongifolia *ramets*
149	
150	Both genet size and elapsed time since fire were significant influences on the proportion of live ramets a lignotuber supported. The proportion of live ramets per genet declined significantly with increasing *H+D* (*r*<sup>2</sup> = 0.12; *F*<sub>1,354</sub> = 47.7, *p* < 0.001). Time since fire added significantly to this regression (*r*<sup>2</sup> = 0.35; *F*<sub>1,354</sub> = 94.7, *p* < 0.001). When the order of fit was reversed the result remained unchanged. 154	#### **Discussion**
155	
156	#### *Population structure in obligate-seeding and resprouting* Banksia *genets*
157	
158	Populations of the obligate-seeder, *B. ericifolia,* were even-aged and therefore well described by the elapsed time since the stand last burnt. Frequency distributions of genet H + D were unimodal. Distributions of this form are common in even-aged populations in which genetic and environmental differences between genets produce differences in relative growth rates over time (Ford, 1975). In contrast, population structures of the resprouter, *B. oblongifolia,* bore little relationship to when the stand last burnt. The wide range of *B. oblongifolia* lignotuber sizes clearly reflects the persistence of genets over an unknown number of past fires (Zammit, 1986). Growth since the last fire, at least as reflected by changes to *H+D,* seems to have little impact on the distribution of sizes in stands of this species.
159	=== PAGE 8 ===
160	18
161	
162	Regeneration after fire in *B. oblongifolia* occurs both by resprouting and by seedling establishment (Siddiqi *et al.,* 1976). It was interesting, therefore, to find a high proportion of small genets in a stand unburnt for 16 years (Fig. 2; 1965). Most of the small *B. oblongifolia* genets found in some transects in the 1965 stand supported single ramets and had small lignotubers (<2 cm diameter) which showed no evidence of fire scars. This suggests an influx of new genets in the absence of fire.
163	
164	Seedling establishment in mature stands has been reported for resprouting species in California coastal sage communities (Malanson & Westman, 1985), and in coastal scrub from southern Australia (Specht *et al.,* 1958). Two different mechanisms might permit the establishment of *B. oblongifolia* seedlings in mature stands. First, seeds released after fire might be dormant and so require further treatment before germinating. There is no evidence of this; *B. oblongifolia* seeds germinate readily (Zammit 1984). Alternatively there might be leakage of seeds from cones between fires. Some *Banksia* follicles, including *B. oblongifolia,* are reported to open in the absence of fire (George, 1981). Whether seed release between fires is an adaptive trait or an accidental consequence of other cone characters remains unclear.
165	
166	The density of *B. ericifolia* genets declined with increasing stand age. Similar mortality patterns occur in even-aged populations of the chaparral obligate-seeder *Ceanothus megacarpus* (Schlesinger & Gill, 1978), even-aged populations of *Ceratiola ericoides* (Johnson, 1982) and monospecific *B. ericifolia* stands in a different heath area on Hawkesbury Sandstone (Morris & Myerscough, 1983).
167	
168	The density of *B. oblongifolia* genets did not vary significantly between stands. Stable densities of resprouters over stands spanning 23 years suggests that populations of this species are not expanding immediately after fire then contracting over time as genets die. Because we did not survey populations during the first 12 months after fire, the time when most new genets are recruited and subsequent mortality occurs (Bradstock & Myerscough, 1981; Zammit, 1986), the impression of relative stability of *B. oblongifolia* numbers reported here excludes the mortality of seedling genets. Nevertheless, these results suggest resprouting *B. oblongifolia* are better able to withstand competitive and other forces which kill established genets.
169	
170	#### *Reproductive status in obligate-seeding and resprouting* Banksia *genets*
171	
172	Resprouting *B. oblongifolia* genets reach sexual maturity sooner than *B. ericifolia* regenerating from seeds. However, the size of resprouting *B. oblongifolia* ramets and *B. ericifolia* genets were similar at first flowering. Pyke (1983) has also reported flower and seed production 2-3 years after fire in resprouting proteaceaous shrubs in this environment. Resprouters in chaparral and garrigue communities begin flowering in the first year after fire and recruit seedlings 2-3 years after fire from the seeds produced (Keeley & Keeley, 1984; Trabaud & de Chanterac, 1985). This contrasts with serotinous species such as *Banksia* which recruit seedlings mostly in the first year after fire (Zammit, 1986). The adaptive significance of this difference is unclear. Possibly the immediate post-fire environment is not the optimal germination time for all species of fire-prone landscapes, or possibly the pattern of flowering and then recruiting seedlings 2-3 years after fire is found where high seed mortality militates against accumulating a seed bank which must be maintained until the next fire.
173	
174	A substantial proportion of resprouting *B. oblongifolia* genets never flowered, a pattern that did not change with increasing time since fire. As in other studies (e.g., Pinero *et al.,* 1982; Grice, 1984), it was always the smallest genets in the population which were not reproductive. If we assume that the smallest *B. oblongifolia* genets are also recent additions to the population, it follows that new genets take more than 23 years to reach reproductive maturity. Observations from glasshouse experiments suggest that lignotubers are formed within 12 months, and lignotubers as small as 1-2 cm in diameter are capable of resprouting (C. Zammit, unpublished data). In the field most genets with lignotuber areas less than about 1.0 dm<sup>2</sup> at the soil surface have never flowered. The requirement for
175	=== PAGE 9 ===
176	19
177	
178	flowering is clearly more than a minimum lignotuber size capable of resprouting.
179	
180	It might reasonably be predicted that genets of the obligate-seeder *B. ericifolia* would produce seeds earlier and more copiously than the resprouter *B. oblongifolia,* for either of two reasons. First lineages of *B. ericifolia* persist through fires by seed only, so they are vulnerable during the period before they develop a seed bank. Selection might be expected to abbreviate this period as much as possible. Second, the resource allocation hypothesis (Harper & Ogden, 1970) argues that as genets develop there are competing demands for limited resources between vegetative and reproductive functions. This has led to the prediction that obligate-seeders ought to produce more seeds than resprouters (Carpenter & Recher, 1979) per unit growth.
181	
182	Considered over the whole life of genets, it appears to be true that *B. ericifolia* produces seed earlier, since *B. oblongifolia* genets did not appear to flower in their first fire cycle. On the other hand within each fire cycle, resprouting *B. oblongifolia* produced seeds sooner, contradicting the argument that obligate-seeders should be selected to seed quickly in order to tolerate short between-fire intervals. Further, there was little evidence that differences between the two species could be attributed to differences in the allocation of resources between growth and reproductive activity. On the contrary, the overall relationship between cone production and H + D was very similar in the two species. The essential difference between the two species seems to lie in the timing of their shoot growth in relation to the fire cycle. The obligate-seeder *B. ericifolia* continues growth much more vigorously than the resprouter *B. oblongifolia* from 5-10 years after fire onwards. On the other hand the resprouter grows more quickly than the obligate-seeder during the first five years after fire, except during the first fire-cycle it experiences as a seedling. Patterns of seed production mirror these patterns of shoot growth, rather than being an alternative activity.
183	
184	For this pair of species it appears that resprouting and obligate-seeding are not alternative ways of dealing with the same fire regime, but are suited to rather different fire regimes. Our data, like those of Benson (1985), suggest *B. ericifolia* would be strongly disadvantaged by short between-fire intervals, and this has recently been observed (Nieuwenhuis, 1985). In contrast, the long-term persistence of *B. oblongifolia* does not seem to be influenced by the frequency of fires. However, the decline in percent live *B. oblongifolia* ramets in the 1958 stand suggests that the absence of a disturbance which stimulates resprouting for extended periods may result in gradual genet senescence.
185

# **Population structure and reproductive status of two** *Banksia* **shrubs at various times after fire**

Charles Zammit<sup>1</sup> & Mark Westoby\*

*School of Biological Sciences, Macquarie University, North Ryde N.S.W. 2113, Australia* 

<sup>1</sup>*Present address: Department of Biology, San Diego State University, San Diego CA 92182, USA* 

Keywords: Australia, *Banksia,* Fire, Population structure, Regeneration strategy, Seed production, Serotiny

# **Abstract**

Populations of the obligate-seeder, *Banksia ericifolia,* were even-aged. Seedling recruitment occurred only after fire. Mean genet size (height + canopy diameter; H + D) increased progressively with elapsed time since fire in stands last burnt 2-23 years before 1981. Populations of a co-occurring resprouter, *B. oblongifolia,* were mixed-aged. Genet size varied significantly between stands, but this variation was not explained by regressions of H + D on years since fire. In addition *B. oblongifolia* seedlings were recruited both after fire and in patches of heath unburnt for 16 years.

Most flower and seed production in *B. oblongifolia* occurred in the stands last burnt less than 10 years previously. More than 30% of genets had not produced cones since the last fire, irrespective of how many years had elapsed. In contrast, few *B. ericifolia* genets had produced cones five years after fire, but by 16 years after fire nearly 100% had. Overall, about 51% of *B. ericifolia* inflorescences and about 28% of *B. oblongifolia* inflorescences set seed. The number of seeds in seed-bearing cones was not significantly different between species.

Resprouting *B. oblongifolia* genets began flowering sooner after fire, but *B. ericifolia* subsequently overtook them in accumulating a bank of serotinous seeds. In the stand unburnt for 23 years the largest *B. ericifolia* genets had more than twice as many cones as the largest co-occurring *B. oblongifolia.* However, when accumulated cone production was compared for genets of equal H + D over all stands, there was no difference between species.

#### **Introduction**

There have been two general approaches to ecological studies of fire effects on vegetation. Community ecologists have monitored regeneration of species assemblages after single fires in Australia (Hill & Read, 1984; Purdie & Slatyer, 1976; Siddiqi *et al.,* 1976; Specht *et al.,* 1958), or studied floristic changes by sampling from communities of known ages (Bell & Koch, 1980; Russell & Parsons, 1978). On the other hand population biologists have examined the effects of fire on population structure (Ashton, 1976; Griffin & Friedel, 1984), seedling recruitment (Bradstock & Myerscough, 1981; Scalan & O'Rourke, 1982) and flowering (Gill & Ingwersen, 1976; Pyke, 1983). A recent volume summarises these and other aspects of the nature, impact and management of fires in the Australian biota (Gill *et al.,* 1981).

<sup>\*</sup> We thank the New South Wales National Parks & Wildlife Service for permission to do this work in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park. We are grateful to Don Adamson, Lynn Day, David Haig and James Sim for constructive comments on earlier drafts.
=== PAGE 2 ===
12

Here we compare the population characteristics, in relation to time elapsed since fire, of two co-occurring *Banksia* (Proteaceae) shrub species common in the fire-prone scrublands of the Sydney Basin. *Banksia ericifolia* L.f. is an obligate-seeder. Individuals (genets) are killed by fire and so depend entirely on successfully recruiting seedlings for the persistence of lineages. Genets are single stemmed and can be up to 5 m tall. Ericoid leaves are arranged in a roughly spherical, continuous canopy, which covers up to 8 m<sup>2</sup> at maturity. In contrast, *B. oblongifolia* Cav. resprouts from a lignotuber after fire. In this species there are two levels of demographic response to fire: the mortality and recruitment of genets (lignotubers) and the mortality and recruitment of ramets (resprouting stems) on each genet. Individual shrubs seldom grow taller than 2 m in the heathlands of the Sydney Basin. However their canopies, made up of discontinuous clusters of large serrate leaves, may span up to 5 m<sup>2</sup>. Both of these *Banksia* shrubs produce a variable number of persistent flowering spikes annually, each of which supports 500-2500+ flowers. A single winged seed is stored in each woody follicle, and follicles are clustered along the flowering spike to form a seed-bearing cone retained in the canopy. Seed release occurs mainly after fire ruptures the follicle, a trait known as serotiny.

Our aim in this comparative survey was to investigate how size frequency distributions and reproductive activity changed during the interval between fires in the two species. By choosing two species which are closely related but differ in the fundamental fire-response characteristic of resprouting vs obligate-seeding, we hoped to develop hypotheses about how other aspects of life history are associated with these characteristics.

#### **Study area and methods**

All surveys were done during March-August 1981 in the Lambert Peninsula region of Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (33°55'S, 151°10'E), about 40 km north of Sydney, Australia. This landscape is part of the Hornsby Plateau, a mid-Triassic formation made up of eroded quartz sandstones interspersed with shales: it supports a number of vegetation types (Thomas & Benson, 1985). Shallow soils, some with impeded drainage, support the heath and scrub (sensu Specht, 1981) common on the plateaus of the peninsula. *Banksia ericifolia* and *B. oblongifolia* are common in the heath, scrub and some woodlands of this region (Thomas & Benson, 1985) and they also co-occur in other sandstone scrublands in the Sydney Basin (Siddiqi *et al.,* 1972).

Fire history records (New South Wales National Parks and Wildlife Service; Northern Metropolitan Office) were used to compile maps of all fire boundaries recorded within the Lambert Peninsula (about 70 km<sup>2</sup>) between 1943-1980. All areas burnt between 1943 and 1957 had been burnt at least once again after 1958. The oldest scrub stand had been unburnt for 23 years. Areas which were last burnt in 1958, 1965, 1973, 1975 and 1979 were selected to represent a time-since-fire sequence. Their boundaries were validated against aerial photographs taken within a few years of the fires (New South Wales Lands Dept. Cumberland series; 1956, 1960, 1970, 1978). This comparison confirmed the overall reliability of the fire records, but highlighted the patchy nature of some fires. The sizes of suitable study areas varied widely. The 1973 and 1975 fires were confined, and only a small portion of the area burnt in 1958 had not been burnt again. The 1965 and 1979 fires burnt through large areas of the park and substantial areas had not been burnt again. Stands which supported both *B. ericifolia* and *B. oblongifolia* and which were similar in topography and vegetation structure were selected as survey sites (Table 1). We chose stands which were on ridgetops or north facing upper slopes. We avoided areas of excessive exposed rock: most transects had less than 10% exposed rock. We generally avoided stands which supported trees, however scattered trees were present in some restricted sites.

Up to five 30 m transects were randomly positioned in each of these sites. Along each transect we examined all plants rooted within 2 m on either side. We recorded height, two maximum canopy diameters, the number of current (1981) inflorescences, the number of seed-bearing cones and the number of barren, old inflorescence spikes. *Banksia ericifolia* at the site last burnt in 1979 were more abundant, and transects 1 m wide were examined. Current inflorescences were always intact. We found no evidence of destruction by insectivorous birds, as reported by Scott & Black (1981) and McFarland (1985).

We could distinguish entire lignotubers for most *B. oblongifolia* genets. However, when this proved difficult because parts of the lignotuber were buried, or when large lignotubers had rotted out in part, we probed the lignotuber perimeter with a metal spike. It is possible that on a few occasions we incorrectly classified several smaller, separate lignotubers as a single larger lignotuber. We counted the number of attached live and dead ramets on each genet.

We calculated several measures of the size of plants, using

13

canopy height, mean canopy diameter, lignotuber area and stem basal area in various combinations. These were all highly intercorrelated (Zammit, 1986). Here we use height plus mean diameter *(H+D)* as a size measure, having found no evidence that other measures were more meaningful. In other perennial species *H+D* is well correlated with plant age and stem diameter (Crisp & Lange, 1976), and with above ground biomass (Grice, 1984). We also harvested seed-bearing cones from nearby individuals of both species and compared their lengths and seed numbers.

In this survey we followed many other workers by examining populations which had been burnt at different times in the past, and interpreting these results as indicating how one population would behave over time. It is desirable to make explicit the reasoning involved. Strictly, our statistics only test for significant differences between different stands created in different fire-years. Because of the restricted area available for some fire-years, we did not study replicate sites within each fire-year. However, even if we had studied replicate sites for each fire, the difficulty would not have been removed, because the sites burnt in any given year are likely to be a very nonrandom sample from all sites. The problem cannot be solved by means of statistics. It is unavoidably a matter of interpretation whether effects are due to differences between site locations, or to differences in time elapsed since fire. Our approach has been to analyse the results in relation to time since fire, and to regard time elapsed as the likely cause when it seems improbable that such a pattern could arise accidentally from differences among site locations. It should be noted that since both species were sampled at the same sites, differences between species cannot be attributed to between-site effects.

#### **Results**

#### *Genet size and reproductive status*

Seed-bearing *B. ericifolia* cones were significantly longer than *B. oblongifolia* (12.2±3.8 cm vs 10.2±2.6 cm, *F*<sub>1,29</sub> = 7.03, *p* < 0.001), however, there was no difference in seed number per cone (*B. ericifolia* 42±20; *B. oblongifolia* 39±16, *F*<sub>1,29</sub> = 0.5, ns). A direct count of the number of seed-bearing cones per genet therefore provided a nondestructive and comparative index of the number of seeds stored in serotinous cones.

In *B. ericifolia* differences among stands in mean H + D, mean cones accumulated, and mean seed-bearing cones accumulated were well described by linear regressions on years since fire (Figs. 1a, b, c). The distribution of *B. ericifolia* H + D size classes between stands followed the expected pattern for the obligate seeding strategy; a single cohort of seedlings was recruited after fire and a new population of genets established (Fig. 2). Sizes of the members of a cohort were normally distributed, but there was wider variance as populations thinned and reached reproductive maturity (Fig. 2). These patterns support the view that populations of the obligate-seeder, *B. ericifolia,* are even-aged.

Mean H + D for *B. oblongifolia* genets did not increase consistently with time since fire. However stands had different frequency distributions of *H+D* (Fig. 2) and different means (Fig. 1a), which may be due to different long term fire histories of particular sites. On the other hand mean cones accumulated and mean seed-bearing cones accumu-
=== PAGE 4 ===
14

*Fig. 1.* Linear regressions of H + D and components of reproductive status on years after fire (x̄±se). (a) Mean H + D of *B. ericifolia* (●) genets increased significantly (H + D = 29.33 + 19.19 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.88, p < 0.001). The sizes of *B. oblongifolia* (○) genets were not influenced by the elapsed time since fire (r<sup>2</sup> = 0.06, ns). (b) Mean cones accumulated (TCP) increased significantly in both species (*B. ericifolia:* TCP = -6.22 + 1.46 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.90, p < 0.013; *B. oblongifolia:* TCP = 2.29 + 0.63 yrs; r<sup>2</sup> = 0.96, p < 0.003).
