#### *Flowering response after fire*

(a) *Response during first spring.* Sixty per cent of species (94 of 157) which regenerated during year 1 flowered or produced spores (Table 5). Of these, 87 species were herbs. The rest included 2 ferns, 2 bryophytes, a fungus and 3 species of shrubs.

About 82% of all herbs recorded (including sedges, rushes, grasses, orchids, lilies, creepers and climbers) flowered in the first year after fire, and almost all the rest by year 2. Some ORR herbs, including autumn and winter-flowering orchids (Acianthus pusillus, Eriochilus cucullatus, Pterostylis parviflora), flowered from 5 months post-fire, as did Drosera whittakeri and Lagenifera gracilis.

There was conspicuous production of fruiting bodies by the moss Funaria hygrometrica, the liverwort Marchantia berteroana, and the fungus Gerronema postii from 6 months post-fire. By late spring, whole hillsides of the open-forest in damp areas (such as subsite E2) were coloured yellowish green by a carpet of fruiting bryophytes.

Grasses were conspicuous in the first spring after fire. Twenty-three species were identified at open-forest sites including 5 species of Danthonia (Table 3). Some species (eg. Danthonia induta and D. procera) flowered prolifically then were not seen in later years. Only 5 species of grasses were recorded in open-forest by year 10 (Table 3).

(b) *Orchid flowering response.* Nineteen species of terrestrial orchids appeared and flowered in
=== PAGE 25 ===
REGENERATION IN THE ANGAHOOK-LORNE STATE PARK 31

open-forest during the first 3 years after fire. Though 16 species of orchids were recorded at subsite E1 during the 10 years, only 4 species appeared and flowered on this dry, eroded slope during year 1 (Table 3). Field observations suggest that the density of year 1 flowering of most species was higher than in pre-fire years.

Flowering of some orchid species was stimulated by fire. Two species (Caladenia menziesii and Prasophyllum odoratum), which appear but rarely flower in normal years, bloomed prolifically the spring after the fire. Seed-set accompanied post-fire flowering for all orchid species during years 1-3.

Only 3 species of orchids (Acianthus pusillus, Pterostylis nana, P. nutans) were recorded in the gully communities prior to the fire and in the 10 years post-fire. Field records made in similar communities near Moggs Creek prior to the fire, list 11 gully species (Acianthus caudatus, A. pusillus, Chiloglottis valida, Corybas dilatatus, C. incurvis, Cyrtostylis reniformis, Pterostylis curta, P. longifolia, P. nana, P. nutans, P. pedunculata— M. White; M. MacDonald, pers. comm.), all of which have been observed in the 10 years post-fire.

(c) *Flowering response of trees and shrubs.* Three shrubs (Goodenia ovata, Pimelea humilis, Lomatia ilicifolia) flowered in the first year. All other shrubs (92%) did not commence flowering till years 2 or 3, or later (Table 5). Lomatia ilicifolia (which is rarely seen to flower except after fire) flowered on new regrowth at 6-8 months. The juvenile phase of some shrubs (eg. Epacris impressa, G. ovata) was brief; flowering occurring within 2 years on plants only a few centimetres high.

By year 3, about two-thirds of the vascular plant species had flowered, including 4 species of trees (Eucalyptus baxteri, E. obliqua, E. tricarpa, E. willisii) and 27 species of shrubs. Not flowering at year 3 were 5 species of trees (Eucalyptus aromaphloia, E. cypellocarpa, E. globulus, E. ovata, E. viminalis), and 7 species of tall shrubs (Acacia dealbata, A. mearnsii, A. melanoxylon, Pomaderris aspera, P. ferruginea, Prostanthera lasianthos, Exocarpus cupressiformis). All 12 species flowered by 10 years post-fire.

By year 3, the percentage of OSR shrubs and OSR herbs flowering was 83% and 97% respectively and most of these species appeared to set seed. Little seed predation was observed either on plants or the soil.

(d) *Grazing during first 3 years.* No grazing of vegetation by native or introduced mammals was seen in the first 2.5 years after fire; though European rabbits (Oryctolagus cuniculus) were observed browsing herbs at subsite E1 late in year 3, and swamp wallabies (Wallabia bicolor) browsing shrubs at subsite E2 during years 7 and 10. Heavy grazing of young shrubs of Goodenia ovata by unidentified insect larvae occurred at all sites during years 1 and 2, with about 50% of the leaves being eaten. Extensive grazing of E. cypellocarpa coppice regrowth (by sawfly larvae, Perga sp.) was seen at subsite E2 during year 3.

#### DISCUSSION

This study has shown that, after a long fire-free interval, an E. tricarpa open-forest in the Anglesea-Aireys Inlet district was resilient to a single severe summer surface wildfire, supporting observations of Gill (1975, 1981) for dry sclerophyll forests in southern Australia.

The regeneration patterns of the open-forest community conform to the 'initial floristic composition' models of Egler (1954), and Purdie & Slatyer (1976), as 99% of vascular plant species present prior to fire re-established during the first three years.

The increase in the number of species of nonvascular plants in both open-forest and gully communities, with time, and as vascular plant cover increased, is similar to that recorded for the Anglesea heaths and heath woodlands (Wark 1996). The decrease in vascular plant species richness, as vascular plant projective cover increased, is similar to that described by Specht and Specht (1989) for sclerophyll communities in southern Australia, and was also observed in the heaths and heath woodlands of the Anglesea area (Wark 1996).

The failure of Amyema pendulum and Hymenophyllum cupressiforme to re-establish in the Ironbark forest and the gully communities respectively in the 10 years following the wildfire is not unexpected. All plants of A. pendulum were killed, and the mistletoe bird, Dicaeum hirundinacium (which is responsible for seed distribution and was uncommon in the Angahook-Lorne State Park before the fire—Conole & Baverstock 1984; Gill 1994), has not been seen in the area in the 10 years since 1983 (P. Reilly, pers. comm.; Reilly 1991). Filmy ferns such as H. cupressiforme, were rare in the district before the fire and probably have not re-established because the climate in the
=== PAGE 26 ===
32 MARGARET C. WARK

gully complexes has become drier. It may take many years for a cool microclimate suitable for these delicate plants to develop. Ashton & Frankenberg (1976) and Chesterfield et al. (1991) have commented that H. cupressiforme is badly affected by wildfire. No H. cupressiforme plants were seen 5 years after the 1983 wildfire in warm temperate rainforest in East Gippsland, Victoria (Chesterfield et al. 1991), and only a few plants 25 years after the 1951 wildfire in cool temperate rainforest at Lily Pilly Gully, Wilsons Promontory National Park, Victoria (D. H. Ashton, pers. comm.).

In the E. tricarpa dry sclerophyll forest, 60% of all species which regenerated following this wildfire were sprouters (FRS or ORR species). Similar high proportions of vegetative regenerators have been described for dry sclerophyll forests in Western Australia (Christensen & Kimber 1975), and the Australian Capital Territory (Purdie & Slatyer 1976). The high proportion (40%) of OSR regenerators seen probably reflects the intensity of the wildfire. It is known that in dry sclerophyll forests in Western Australia and New South Wales high intensity fires stimulate germination of hard-seeded understorey shrubs and fireweeds (Christensen & Kimber 1975; Christensen et al. 1981; Auld & O'Connell 1991). The dense shrub understoreys (dominated by Acacia and Pultenaea spp.) which established throughout most of the open-forest communities of the Anglesea-Aireys Inlet region following the Ash Wednesday wildfire, replaced the previously more open, often grassy, understorey (Parsons et al. 1977). Field records (Pat Denham, pers. comm.) suggest that the seed which germinated forming the shrub understorey in the E. tricarpa open-forest may have been stored in the soil for over 30 years—possibly longer if previous fires were of insufficient intensity to stimulate germination.

The slow rate of crown recovery of the E. tricarpa open-forest in the first three years after fire, may have been a result of both moisture stress, and low nutrient status. Leitch et al. (1983) showed increased hydrophobic properties of the soil at a forest site near Warburton, Victoria, where extensive sheet erosion (and resulting soil nutrient losses) occurred following the Ash Wednesday wildfires. They commented that similar sheet erosion also occurred in some of the Otway forests following the Ash Wednesday fires, and our data supports this.

Both moisture and nutrients released from ash are necessary for establishment of early post-fire bryophyte colonisers such as M. berteroana, F. hygrometrica and C. purpureus (G. A. M. Scott, pers. comm.; Cremer & Mount 1965; Southorn 1977), and stimulate post-fire flowering in orchids (Pate & Dixon 1982). The reduced incidence of the early post-fire bryophytes at subsite E1, and the failure of 75% of the orchid species at this site to flower in the first year after fire, suggest that both moisture and certain nutrients were lacking in these exposed sites. In 1983, Barnett (1984) noted a decrease in flowering of some orchid species following a surface fire in a Eucalyptus macrorhyncha open-forest, on a steep site with heavy clay soils at King Lake, Victoria, and suggested that one factor which may have affected flowering was the removal, by soil erosion, of fire-released nutrients. Changes in the soil microflora after the fire may also have been a factor. Similarly, the failure of the parasitic tall shrub E. cupressiformis to survive on these dry sites after its early re-establishment from seed and by regrowth, suggests also that insufficient moisture and nutrients may have been available to the young plants in the early years after fire.

The open-forest described in the present paper may not be totally resilient to frequent severe wildfires if burning occurs before the primary juvenile period of some OSR species. In the Ironbark forest, 3 species of OSR tall shrubs (Acacia mearnsii, A. dealbata, Pomaderris ferruginea) had neither flowered nor set seed 3 years after the fire. If another fire occurred before they reached reproductive maturity, they could be eliminated. Parsons et al. (1977) have commented that repeated burning at frequent intervals may convert an open-forest with a shrub understorey to an open-forest with a grassy understorey. Coaldrake (1961) has observed similar changes following sequential fires in the coastal lowlands of southern Queensland.

In the gully complexes (where peat fires did not occur) 52% of the species which regenerated following the wildfire were OSR species, regenerating from seed only. Similar high proportions (50-60%) of obligate seed regenerators have been described for wet sclerophyll forests in Western Australia (Christensen & Kimber 1975), Victoria and New South Wales (Ashton 1981). The regeneration patterns of the Anglesea gully communities (in the absence of peat fires) also conformed to the initial floristic composition models of Egler (1954) and Purdie and Slatyer (1976) as 99% of vascular plant species present prior to the fire re-established during the first 3 years.

Like the E. tricarpa open-forest, the gully communities (where peat did not burn) may not be totally resilient to frequent severe wildfires.
=== PAGE 27 ===
REGENERATION IN THE ANGAHOOK-LORNE STATE PARK 33

By year 3, at least 4 OSR shrubs in each gully community had not flowered or set seed, including Pomaderris aspera and Prostanthera lasianthos. Seed of these species is stored in the soil, and Pomaderris aspera may be removed from an area if surface fires recur at intervals of less than 5-10 years (Ashton & Attiwill 1994). Burning of these areas twice within the primary juvenile period of these shrubs could result in their elimination.

The study has also shown that such dry gully communities may be extremely vulnerable to wildfire and that their floristics and structure may change dramatically if peat fires establish. In the 10 years following the peat fire, the E. obliqua gully complex with its Prostanthera lasianthos, Cyathea australis understorey has become a eucalypt monoculture with practically no understorey. It is likely that the seed source for recolonisation of the burnt peat was the surrounding E. obliqua/E. willisii open-forest, which contained 20 m eucalypts which had flowered and set seed the season before the wildfire. It was shown, after the Anglesea wildfires, that viable seed could survive in capsules of crown-fired E. obliqua (Ashton 1986). It is probable that seed shedding occurred onto the surface of the burnt peat after the in-ground fire was extinguished. Seeding in of Spyridium parvifolium probably also occurred from the surrounding open-forest. The presence of this shrub suggests the microclimate in both gully communities at site F is now drier than before the surface fire and the peat fire.

Hill & Read (1984) showed that the proximity of a sclerophyll seed source may result in significant changes in the species composition of the understorey of mixed eucalypt forests following humus fires in western Tasmania. They observed that species of sclerophyllous shrubs (Leptospermum scoparium, Phebalium squameum) found 150-400 m from their study area established from wind-dispersed seed on burnt peat.

In the present study it was found that, with the exception of two FRS species (Pteridium esculentum, Tetrarrhena juncea) which grew into the burnt peat after the fire ceased, all 12 other species of vascular plants found on the burnt peat at year 10 established from seed or spores shed into the area from the adjacent gully complex, or surrounding dry sclerophyll forest.

Because of the density of the eucalypt overstorey, and the changed hydrology of the area, it may be many decades, or even some hundreds of years, before an understorey of Prostanthera lasianthos and Cyathea australis re-establishes in the area of the peat fire. Burning of this area at 10 years, by either a low intensity fire or a wildfire, could result in reduction or elimination of any OSR gully species which have begun to re-establish, and the continued invasion of sclerophyllous species from the adjacent E. obliqua open-forest.

It is probable that the red material produced when the peat burnt had certain properties which favoured plant establishment and growth in the short term. A dense cover of ash-requiring mosses and liverworts (including F. hygrometrica, C. purpureus and M. berteroana—Southorn 1977) appeared on the burnt peat in the first 3 years after fire. Cremer & Mount (1965) and Duncan & Dalton (1982) have described a similar sequence of bryophyte colonisation following felling and burning of E. regnans forests in Tasmania.

Pot experiments comparing burnt and unburnt peat showed that E. obliqua grew rapidly on burnt peat and then became chlorotic, probably due to nutrient imbalance or toxicity. Similar observations of chlorosis and poor growth have been made by Smith (1983) for Acacia dealbata growing on red burnt soils (derived from intense sustained log fires).

However, any nutrient imbalance of the burnt soil resulting from the peat fire did not prevent establishment of eucalypt seedlings, whose height at 3 years (5.0 m) equalled that of seedlings growing on unburnt peat in open areas, in the gully nearby. It is possible that increased light and a reduction of allelopathic factors in the soil, following burning of the peat, may have also contributed to the dense and rapid growth of eucalypt seedlings on the burnt peat. Once the seedlings on burnt peat (subsite F2) reached the 2.0 m water table (at 2-3 years), their growth appeared faster than that of seedlings on unburnt peat soil in the adjacent gully complex (subsite F1).

Though peat fires are relatively rare in mainland Australia (Gill 1981), the present study indicates that they may cause significant changes in vegetation structure and floristics in some gully communities. In the present study, no resilience was shown by an E. obliqua/ P. lasianthos/C. australis gully community where a peat (ground) fire developed following a surface wildfire, as all the plants present at the time of the peat fire (including their buried seeds and propagules) were killed at or below ground level.

Similar lack of resilience has been reported following peat fires in Melaleuca squarrosa closed scrub on the humus-rich soil of the river valleys to the north and west of Anglesea with consequential changes in vegetation structure and floristics (Gill 1993; White 1994), and replacement
=== PAGE 28 ===
34 MARGARET C. WARK

of the M. squarrosa closed scrub by a Eucalyptus aromaphloia woodland. The present study indicates that, in Victoria, peat fires may occasionally cause significant changes in vegetation structure and floristics. Management strategies are required to prevent and control in-ground fires, especially when they establish in communities of ecological significance (Gill 1993, 1994).

3	# CSIRO **Publishing**
4	
5	# AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL *of* BOTANY

14

18

20	=== PAGE 2 ===
21	*Aust. J. Bot.*, 2002, **50**, 545–557
22	
23	## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**
24	
25	*Andrew J. Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D. Auld*
26	
27	Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.
28	
29	<sup>A</sup>Corresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au
30	
31	*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D. excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T. speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D. excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T. speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D. excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T. speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.
32	
33	Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D. excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T. speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D. excelsa*) or 3 m (*T. speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T. speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.
34	
35	For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D. excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T. speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D. excelsa* (two sites) and *T. speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T. speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.
36	
37	#### **Introduction**
38	
39	In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and non-leguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).
40	
41	However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 
42	
43	© CSIRO 2002 10.1071/BT02009 0067-1924/02/050545
44	=== PAGE 3 ===
45	546 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld
46	
47	the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.
48	
49	Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X. fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T. speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.
50	
51	In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).
52	
53	In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.
54	
55	#### **Methods**
56	
57	#### *Study species*
58	
59	*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).
60	
61	*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.
62	
63	#### *Sites*
64	
65	Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D. excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E. sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T. speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E. sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).
66	
67	All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D. excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).
68	
69	#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
70	
71	The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.
72	
73	#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*
74	
75	Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D. excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T. speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact
76	=== PAGE 4 ===
77	Reproduction in two pyrogenic flowerers 547
78	
79	follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T. speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D. excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T. speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D. excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m<sup>2</sup>).
80	
81	To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T. speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.
82	
83	#### *Primary seed dispersal*
84	
85	The seeds of *D. excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T. speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T. speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D. excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.
86	
87	The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D. excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T. speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D. excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D. excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T. speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T. speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.
88	
89	#### *Seed predation*
90	
91	The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D. excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:
92	
93	(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.
94	
95	(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.
96	
97	Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.
98	
99	The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.
100	
101	Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D. excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T. speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.
102	
103	#### *Seedling dispersal*
104	
105	The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:
106	
107	(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D. excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T. speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.
108	
109	(b) for *D. excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T. speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.
110	
111	#### *Analyses*
112	
113	To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D. excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T. speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m<sup>2</sup> were compared in *D. excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T. speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).
114	
115	To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation
116	=== PAGE 5 ===
117	548 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld
118	
119	exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.
120	
121	At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T. speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D. excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D. excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T. speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).
122	
123	We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T. speciosissima*. In *D. excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T. speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.
124	
125	For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).
126	
127	To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.
128	
129	(i) For *D. excelsa* at Site 1, seed and seedling data from the isolated plants were placed into 0.1-m classes and frequency counts of seeds or seedlings were obtained from each distance class for all five individuals. The proportions of seeds or seedlings per distance class were then determined. Seedling data for distances less than 0.25 m from the adult were omitted, since data for seed distribution were not obtained at this distance, due to the occupation of most of the available space by the parent plants. Similarly, seedling distances greater than 7.15 m were omitted since this was distance of the furthest observed seed. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to determine the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distribution (observed) with the seed distribution (predicted) (Zar 1996).
130	
131	(ii) For *D. excelsa* at Site 1 and *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, estimations were made of the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distributions from the plot transect sampling (observed) with the seed distributions from the isolated individuals (expected). Restriction of seedling data to the greatest distance observed for seeds (7.15 m) was as above for *D. excelsa*, and to 3.75 m for *T. speciosissima*. There was no restriction on the least distance for *T. speciosissima*. This test enabled the determination of whether the distribution of seeds around isolated adults adequately explained the distribution of seedlings around adults that were contagiously distributed (a more typical situation) and thus had overlapping seed shadows.
132	
133	(iii) For *D. excelsa* at Site 1, the seedling distribution from the five isolated plants ('expected') was compared with that obtained from the plot transect sampling ('observed'). This test assessed how well the distribution of seedlings around isolated plants of *D. excelsa* represented the more typical situation of contagiously distributed individuals.
134	
135	#### **Results**
136	
137	#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*
138	
139	For both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D. excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T. speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T. speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.
140	
141	#### *Fruit and seed production*
142	
143	In *D. excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m<sup>–2</sup>) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m<sup>–2</sup>) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T. speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T. speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T. speciosissima* (*F*<sub>1,46</sub> = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D. excelsa* (*F*<sub>1,42</sub> = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D. excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). The lack of significance in this comparison is likely to be a result of the considerable variation between plots at Site 2, with one plot producing approximately 1.5 times as many seeds as the other. This in turn was largely because of the much higher density of flowering and fruiting plants in plot 2 than in plot 1 of Site 2 (Table 1). There were no significant differences in seed density of *T. speciosissima* between sites (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 1.11, *P* = 0.40) or among years (*F*<sub>2,2</sub> = 4.19, *P* = 0.19). In the first post-fire fruiting year (1996), the estimated density of seeds

*Aust. J. Bot.*, 2002, **50**, 545–557

## **Flowering, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling recruitment in two pyrogenic flowering resprouters**

*Andrew J. Denham*<sup>A</sup> *and Tony D. Auld*

Biodiversity Research Group, NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, PO Box 1967, Hurstville, NSW 2220, Australia.

<sup>A</sup>Corresponding author; email: andrew.denham@npws.nsw.gov.au

*Abstract.* A few resprouting plants in fire-prone environments have no local seed bank (soil or canopy) when a fire occurs. These species rely on post-fire flowering and the production of non-dormant seeds to exploit favourable post-fire establishment and growth conditions. For two such pyrogenic flowering species (*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa and *Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br.), we examined the timing of seed release, patterns of fruit production, seed dispersal, seed predation and seedling establishment following a fire in the Sydney region of southeastern Australia. Both species took some 19 months after the fire to flower and the first seeds were released 2 years after the fire. *D. excelsa* flowered and fruited only once after the fire. For *T. speciosissima*, plants also flowered at least once more in the subsequent 5 years, but produced seed in only the first three post-fire flowering years. Fruit production differed between species, with fruiting individuals of *D. excelsa* producing fewer infructescences, similar numbers of follicles, but many more seeds per follicle than fruiting individuals of *T. speciosissima*. Ultimately, *D. excelsa* produced approximately six times as many seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and four times as many seeds per adult in one flowering season than *T. speciosissima* did after four flowering (three successful fruiting) seasons.

Seeds were passively dispersed from fruits borne 3–4 m (*D. excelsa*) or 1–2 m (*T. speciosissima*) above the ground. Most seeds were found within 5 m (*D. excelsa*) or 3 m (*T. speciosissima*) of parent plants. The primary seed shadow of both species was a poor predictor of the distribution of seedlings, with more seedlings occurring further from the adults than expected from the distribution of seeds. Seed loss to predators was high in both species in exclusion experiments where mammals had access to clumps of seeds (77–88%). It was variable and generally lower (8–65%) in experiments where seeds were not locally clumped. However, for *T. speciosissima*, at one site, some 65% of seeds were lost to mammals and invertebrates in these latter experiments. At this site, these losses appeared to influence subsequent recruitment levels, as very low seedling densities were observed.

For both species, germination of seedlings first occurred some 2.5–3 years after the passage of the fire. The percentage of seeds produced to seedlings successfully established was low in *D. excelsa* (2–3%) and more variable across sites and years in *T. speciosissima* (0–18%). Resultant post-fire seedling densities of *D. excelsa* (two sites) and *T. speciosissima* at one site were similar, but they were much lower at the *T. speciosissima* site that had high levels of seed predation. Both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* are amongst the slowest woody resprouting species to recruit seedlings after fire in south-eastern Australia and lag years behind species with soil or canopy seed banks.

#### **Introduction**

In fire-prone habitats, recruitment in plant species is frequently linked to the passage of a fire (Tyler 1995). This results from at least two main mechanisms. First, in species with soil seed banks, seed dormancy may be broken by the passage of fires (e.g. via heat, smoke, charred wood: Keeley 1991; Brown 1993; or interactions of these factors: Keith 1997; Morris 2000). Examples include many legumes (Jeffery *et al.* 1988; Auld and O'Connell 1991) and non-leguminous species (Brown 1993; Dixon *et al.* 1995). Second, in species with canopy seed banks, fires result in the mass opening of fruits and the release of seeds (Bond *et al.* 1984; Lamont *et al.* 1991).

However, a number of species have no available seed storage in either the soil or canopy at the time of the passage of a fire (Keith 1996). A few may rely on dispersal from unburnt areas, but most have mechanisms that allow established plants to survive fire via buried lignotubers, rhizomes or buds (protected meristems). These species usually flower soon after fire and then release seeds (Gill 1981; Frost 1984; Johnson *et al.* 1994; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Carrington 1999). For species dependant on post-fire flowering for recruitment (pyrogenic flowering resprouters), 

© CSIRO 2002 10.1071/BT02009 0067-1924/02/050545
=== PAGE 3 ===
546 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld

the timing and magnitude of this flowering will influence opportunities for post-fire seedling establishment. The longer the interval between the passage of a fire and seedling recruitment, the more of the available resources such as light, nutrients and space, are likely to have been captured by other resprouting species or by those species with soil or canopy seed banks that can recruit in the immediate post-fire period.

Many individuals of pyrogenic flowering resprouting species in south-eastern Australia appear to have a single post-fire flowering (e.g. *Angophora hispida*, Auld 1986; *Blandfordia nobilis*, Johnson *et al.* 1994; *Lomatia silaifolia*, Denham and Whelan 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Gill and Ingwersen 1976, but see; *X. fulva*, Taylor *et al.* 1998). In such cases, this represents the only opportunity for recruitment between fires. For other species, flowering may extend over several years following a fire (e.g. *T. speciosissima*, Pyke 1983; Bradstock 1995; Goldingay 2000; *Xanthorrhoea australis*, Curtis 1998). However, the timing of recruitment in pyrogenic flowering resprouting species has been little studied and the degree to which each post-fire flowering event contributes to recruitment is unexplored.

In the post-fire environment, the impact of seed predation may be reduced due to lower predator abundance and also via predator satiation, in the case of serotinous seed release (Whelan 1995; Bond and van Wilgen 1996; Myerscough *et al.* 2000). However, the seeds of pyrogenic flowering resprouters are likely to be released after most seeds from serotinous species have germinated and, consequently, would not benefit from any predator satiation effects from serotinous seed release. In addition, populations of predators may have recovered by this time. All pyrogenic flowering resprouters are thought to release seeds in a non-dormant state (Bell *et al.* 1993; Bond and van Wilgen 1996) and hence form transient soil seed banks (*sensu* Parker and Kelly 1989).

In this study, we assessed post-fire reproduction and the patterns of seedling recruitment after a wildfire in 1994, in two resprouting species reliant on post-fire flowering for seed production (*Doryanthes excelsa* and *Telopea speciosissima*), from the Sydney area of south-eastern Australia. We examined (i) the timing of flowering and magnitude of seed production over 5 years after the fire; (ii) the pattern of seed and seedling dispersal; (iii) the level of post-dispersal seed predation; and (iv) the proportion of seeds released that resulted in successful establishment of new plants.

#### **Methods**

#### *Study species*

*Doryanthes excelsa* Correa (Gymea lily—Doryanthaceae) is a large perennial rosette plant with a bulbous rhizome and long broad linear leaves up to 3 m long. It is apparently capable of asexual reproduction by branching of the rhizome (Nash 1996). It grows in dry sclerophyll forests and woodlands on soils derived from sandstone containing some clay and is restricted to the Sydney Basin in south-eastern Australia, with three outlying populations in northern New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having apical buds protected in underground leaf bases. It flowers in a large, red inflorescence held up to 5 m above the foliage of the plant (Harden 1990–1993). Fire appears to stimulate flowering, although sporadic flowering does occur in the absence of fire (Nash 1996). The mechanism determining flowering is unknown (Beeh 1996; Nash 1996).

*Telopea speciosissima* (Smith) R.Br. (waratah—Proteaceae) is a tall shrub, generally 2–4 m, which is also known for its striking red blooms that emerge above the resprouting shrubby vegetation in the post-fire environment. It is common in dry sclerophyll forest and woodlands on the central coast and central and southern tablelands of New South Wales (Harden 1990–1993). The species survives fire by having dormant buds protected in an underground lignotuber (Bradstock 1995). Aerial stems are completely regrown after each fire.

#### *Sites*

Three sample sites within a 10-km radius were chosen in Royal National Park, about 35 km south of Sydney (34°03′S, 151°03′E). All sites occurred on soils derived from the Triassic Hawkesbury Sandstone Formation, although Site 1 (with an ironstone influence) and Site 2 (with an alluvial influence) were on soils slightly more fertile than Site 3. At Site 1, both study species occurred in ironstone woodland vegetation (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Eucalyptus sieberi*, *Corymbia gummifera*, *Banksia serrata*, *Xylomelum pyriforme* and *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*. The shrubby understorey included *Grevillea diffusa*, *Banksia spinulosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa*, *Prostanthera* sp., *Isopogon anemonifolius*, *Acacia myrtifolia*, *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Lomandra* spp. and *Dianella* sp. The vegetation at Site 2 (*D. excelsa* only) is Sandstone Gully Forest (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with an overstorey of *Angophora costata*, *Banksia serrata*, *Ceratopetalum gummiferum*, *Eucalyptus piperita* and *E. sieberi* and a shrubby understorey that included *Boronia pinnata*, *Grevillea mucronulata*, *Acacia terminalis*, *Lomandra longifolia* and *Caustis flexuosa*. At Site 3 (*T. speciosissima* only) the vegetation is Sandstone Heath (D. Keith and M. Tozer, unpubl. data), with a short overstorey of *Corymbia gummifera*, *Eucalyptus obstans*, *E. sclerophylla* and *Banksia serrata* and a shrubby understorey that included *Lambertia formosa*, *Lissanthe strigosa* and sedges including *Xanthorrhoea media*, *Restio dimorpha* and *Cyathochaeta diandra*. Plant nomenclature follows Harden (1990–1993).

All sites were burnt in January 1994. Before 1994, there was variation in fire history across sites. The eastern part of Site 1 (sampled for *D. excelsa*) and Site 3 were burnt in 1988. The western part of Site 1, separated by a road from the eastern part (sampled for both study species), and Site 2 were burnt in the early 1980s (NPWS fire records; D. Keith, pers. comm.).

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

The three study sites were monitored to observe flowering after the January 1994 fire for both species up until December 2000. As both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* flower in July–October, this involved seven potential flowering seasons (1994–2000). General observations were also made throughout Royal National Park to determine whether the pattern of the study sites was representative of the general response of the study species to fire in this area. The timing of fruit development and seed release was recorded for the first four flowering seasons after the 1994 fire.

#### *Estimates of seed production and seedling establishment*

Six 30 × 30-m plots were established as follows: *D. excelsa*, two plots at each of Sites 1 and 2; *T. speciosissima*, one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. For both study species, within each plot at each site, the numbers of infructescences and follicles on all plants were scored each year (1994–2000). To estimate the number of seeds per follicle, intact
=== PAGE 4 ===
Reproduction in two pyrogenic flowerers 547

follicles were collected in autumn 1996, prior to dehiscence, for each species from each site. For *T. speciosissima*, samples of 23 and 25 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 3, respectively, while for *D. excelsa*, samples of 15 and 29 follicles were collected from Sites 1 and 2, respectively. Seeds within these follicles were scored after dehiscence in the laboratory. For *T. speciosissima*, only those seeds judged as 'filled' (i.e. likely to be viable) were included in this assessment (see also Bradstock 1995; Denham and Whelan 2000). For *D. excelsa*, no assessment was made, although Nash (1996) found that the average viability of seeds collected from a number of locations (not including Royal National Park) was 86% (±6.2 s.e.). The individuals used to estimate numbers of seeds per follicle were sampled from outside the plots to avoid impacts on primary seed dispersal and seedling recruitment. The density of seeds per plot was estimated by multiplying the number of intact follicles by the estimate of the mean number of seeds per follicle and dividing this value by the area of each plot (900 m<sup>2</sup>).

To estimate the magnitude of post-fire seedling recruitment for both study species, five randomly allocated transects each 1 × 30 m were searched for seedlings in spring 1998, within each of the 30 × 30-m plots. For *T. speciosissima*, we assessed the probable fruiting year from which seedlings were established, by comparisons with other seedlings of known age within the sites.

#### *Primary seed dispersal*

The seeds of *D. excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). The seeds of *T. speciosissima* are winged and weigh approximately 72 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T. speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D. excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.

The spatial pattern of initial seed fall was estimated by counting seeds found on the ground in four orthogonal transects along compass bearings from each of five isolated plants at Site 1 for *D. excelsa* and Sites 1 and 3 for *T. speciosissima*. Because of time constraints, this was not done at Site 2 for *D. excelsa*. Searches were done in June–August of 1996, when most seeds had fallen from the follicles. Some further redistribution of seeds along the soil surface by wind and rain after this time is likely (Lamont *et al.* 1993; Hammill *et al.* 1998). The transects for *D. excelsa* started approximately 0.25 m from the centre of each clump, because of the space occupied by the leaf bases of the plants. Counts of numbers of seeds were made every 0.1 m along each transect. Transects were 0.5 m wide and limited to 7.25 m long as there were no seeds seen in initial searches beyond 7.15 m. For *T. speciosissima*, the area occupied by the stems was included in the transects. In preliminary searches around *T. speciosissima* adults, no seeds were found more than 3 m from adults at Site 1 and 2 m from adults at Site 3, so the transect lengths were reduced to 3.5 and 2.5 m, respectively.

#### *Seed predation*

The fates of recently released seeds on the ground were examined during the initial seed release after the 1994 fire (i.e. in 1996), in two trials. First, an exclusion experiment was used to investigate the agents responsible for and the degree of post-dispersal predation at each site. It was assumed that no secondary dispersal of seeds by invertebrates such as ants was likely, since neither species have lipid bodies attached to their seeds. Westoby *et al.* (1990) suggested that neither species is myrmecochorous and field observations supported this. A block design was used with two treatments and 10 seeds per treatment per block. This experiment was set up for *D. excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and for *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3 as follows:

(a) caged: cages (15 × 15 cm × 5 cm high with 1-cm<sup>2</sup> mesh size) were used to exclude vertebrate predators, while still allowing access to most invertebrates. To prevent seeds from washing away in heavy rain, a PVC ring sawn from pipe 10 cm in diameter and about 1 cm tall was placed on the ground. This ring was pushed into the soil leaving only the top 0.5 cm protruding. The cage was placed over the ring and fastened down with wire stakes.

(b) uncaged: where only the PVC ring was used. This allowed access to both invertebrates and vertebrates.

Ten blocks consisting of a caged and an uncaged treatment, were used for each species, at each site. The blocks were placed about 5 m apart along a transect through the site, with separate transects for each species at Site 1.

The number of seeds remaining in each treatment block was recorded every day for the first week and approximately every second day for the following 10 weeks. Additionally, any information concerning the condition of seeds (such as whether chewed or germinated) or the presence of testa remains was recorded at each visit.

Second, for both study species, a trial was established to examine the level of predation on seeds that were placed singly at random locations throughout the plots, rather than clumped as above (see Auld and Denham 1999, 2001). These trials were established for *D. excelsa* in two plots at Site 1 and in one plot at Site 2 and for *T. speciosissima* in one plot at each of Sites 1 and 3. A single seed was placed at each of 10 randomly located positions according to the 30 × 30-m grid established at each site, with the location marked by a steel stake 0.2 m away. Additional batches of 10 seeds were similarly placed in new random locations each week for the following 3 weeks. The fate of these seeds was followed for the next 10 weeks, with details recorded as for the exclusion experiment. Only 'filled' seeds were used in these experiments.

#### *Seedling dispersal*

The following two different estimates were made of the dispersal pattern of seedlings around adult plants:

(a) the ground was searched for seedlings up to a distance of 10 m from fruiting plants around five isolated plants of *D. excelsa* at Site 1. The distance of each seedling from the centre of the adult was measured. The adults included two of those used to sample primary seed dispersal. Sufficient seedlings were not available at the other three adults sampled for primary seed dispersal. For *T. speciosissima*, this technique was not used as adults continued to flower after the first year.

(b) for *D. excelsa* at Sites 1 and 2 and *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, the distance of each seedling from the centre of the nearest parent was measured for all seedlings observed in the transects used for estimating seedling establishment (above). Because of the overall low number of seedlings observed for *T. speciosissima* at Site 3, the entire 30 × 30-m plot was surveyed. This estimate included overlapping seed shadows from adult plants, as typically occurs in the field.

#### *Analyses*

To test the hypothesis that fruit and seed production varied across sites and years within the study area, estimates of infructescence and follicle production per fruiting plant were compared in *D. excelsa* by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested within sites and in *T. speciosissima* across sites and years when fruit was produced, by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication. Estimates of seed production per m<sup>2</sup> were compared in *D. excelsa* across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA with plots as replicates and in *T. speciosissima* across sites and fruiting years by a 2-factor ANOVA without replication (Zar 1996).

To test the hypothesis that vertebrate seed predators had an impact on the number of seeds available for germination (the seed predation
=== PAGE 5 ===
548 A. J. Denham and T. D. Auld

exclusion experiment), the proportions of seeds remaining in each replicate treatment within the 10 blocks after 75 days were compared by a 3-factor ANOVA (factors were treatment, site and block, with blocks nested within sites) for each species separately. The hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1, where both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima* were sampled, was tested by a 3-factor ANOVA with species and caging treatment (with blocks nested within species) as factors.

At lower seed densities than in the seed predation exclusion experiment (the single seeds trial) we tested the hypothesis that predation varied across sites. For *T. speciosissima*, the proportions of seeds remaining in each weekly cohort of 10 seeds at the end of the study (after 9 weeks) were compared across sites by a 1-factor ANOVA. Data for *D. excelsa* were similarly analysed, using both plots at Site 1 and the single plot at Site 2 as three levels in a 'location' factor. Again, it was possible to test the hypothesis that the two species suffered different levels of predation at Site 1 at this lower seed density. Here, only the western of the two *D. excelsa* plots was used, as it was adjacent to the *T. speciosissima* plot (1-factor ANOVA).

We tested the hypothesis that seedling establishment varied across sites in both species and across years for *T. speciosissima*. In *D. excelsa*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites by a nested 2-factor ANOVA with plots nested in sites. For *T. speciosissima*, the number of seedlings per transect was compared across sites and fruiting year of origin by a 2-factor ANOVA.

For each ANOVA, homogeneity of variances was tested by Cochran's test. Where variances were significantly heterogeneous an arcsine transformation was applied to proportion data and a square-root transformation was applied to count data. If variances were still heterogeneous, the analysis was carried out on the raw data with a conservative approach to rejection of the null hypothesis (Underwood 1981).

To test the hypothesis that the distributions of seedlings around plants were the same as the distributions of seeds around plants, a number of Kolmogorov–Smirnov goodness-of-fit tests were done.

(i) For *D. excelsa* at Site 1, seed and seedling data from the isolated plants were placed into 0.1-m classes and frequency counts of seeds or seedlings were obtained from each distance class for all five individuals. The proportions of seeds or seedlings per distance class were then determined. Seedling data for distances less than 0.25 m from the adult were omitted, since data for seed distribution were not obtained at this distance, due to the occupation of most of the available space by the parent plants. Similarly, seedling distances greater than 7.15 m were omitted since this was distance of the furthest observed seed. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test was used to determine the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distribution (observed) with the seed distribution (predicted) (Zar 1996).

(ii) For *D. excelsa* at Site 1 and *T. speciosissima* at Sites 1 and 3, estimations were made of the goodness-of-fit of the seedling distributions from the plot transect sampling (observed) with the seed distributions from the isolated individuals (expected). Restriction of seedling data to the greatest distance observed for seeds (7.15 m) was as above for *D. excelsa*, and to 3.75 m for *T. speciosissima*. There was no restriction on the least distance for *T. speciosissima*. This test enabled the determination of whether the distribution of seeds around isolated adults adequately explained the distribution of seedlings around adults that were contagiously distributed (a more typical situation) and thus had overlapping seed shadows.

(iii) For *D. excelsa* at Site 1, the seedling distribution from the five isolated plants ('expected') was compared with that obtained from the plot transect sampling ('observed'). This test assessed how well the distribution of seedlings around isolated plants of *D. excelsa* represented the more typical situation of contagiously distributed individuals.

#### **Results**

#### *Timing of flowering and seed release*

For both *D. excelsa* and *T. speciosissima*, the first flowering after the January 1994 fires occurred in late winter (August) of 1995, some 19 months after the January 1994 fire. This pattern was found at all study sites and more generally across Royal National Park. Fruits matured in the following autumn (March–June 1996), with *D. excelsa* first releasing seeds in March 1996 and *T. speciosissima* in April 1996. Consequently, seeds were not released into the post-fire habitat until some 25–26 months after the passage of the January 1994 fire. Seed fall was quite prolonged with some seeds still in fruits in June (both species). *D. excelsa* plants in the study plots did not flower in any of the subsequent 5 years, while most *T. speciosissima* individuals flowered again the following year and a few in three of the subsequent 4 years (Table 1), with a similar timing of flowering and fruiting to that observed in 1995–1996.

#### *Fruit and seed production*

In *D. excelsa*, the number, and hence density, of flowering plants varied considerably between plots within sites, ranging from six at Site 1, plot 1 (0.2 m<sup>–2</sup>) to 39 at Site 2, plot 2 (1.3 m<sup>–2</sup>) (Table 1). There were no significant differences between sites in the mean numbers of infructescences (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 0.86, *P* = 0.45) or follicles (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 9.94, *P* = 0.09) produced per fruiting plant, although there were almost twice as many follicles produced at Site 1, plot 1, than at Site 2, plot 2 (Table 1). For *T. speciosissima*, the total number of individuals that flowered between 1995 and 2000 varied from 14 at Site 1 to 24 at Site 3 (Table 1). There was no significant difference in the mean number of infructescences (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 0.4, *P* = 0.59) or follicles (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 0.003, *P* = 0.96) per fruiting plant between sites across the 1995–1997 flowering seasons. *D. excelsa* had greater seed production per follicle than *T. speciosissima* (104, 105 *v.* 11 seeds per follicle, respectively, Table 2). There were no significant differences in the number of seeds per follicle between sites for *T. speciosissima* (*F*<sub>1,46</sub> = 0.43, *P* = 0.52) or *D. excelsa* (*F*<sub>1,42</sub> = 0.08, *P* = 0.93) (Table 2). The estimated density of seeds produced by *D. excelsa* varied greatly, although not significantly (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 4.76, *P* = 0.16) across sites, with Site 1 producing 9.9 (±0.4 s.e.) seeds per m<sup>2</sup> and Site 2 producing 17.7 (±3.6 s.e.) (Table 3). The lack of significance in this comparison is likely to be a result of the considerable variation between plots at Site 2, with one plot producing approximately 1.5 times as many seeds as the other. This in turn was largely because of the much higher density of flowering and fruiting plants in plot 2 than in plot 1 of Site 2 (Table 1). There were no significant differences in seed density of *T. speciosissima* between sites (*F*<sub>1,2</sub> = 1.11, *P* = 0.40) or among years (*F*<sub>2,2</sub> = 4.19, *P* = 0.19). 92:The seeds of *D. excelsa* are disc-like, about 15 mm in diameter, 2 mm thick, have a dry spongy texture and weigh approximately 43 mg (Westoby *et al.* 1990; Nash 1996; A. J. Denham, pers. obs.). Westoby *et al.* (1990) considered *T. speciosissima* to be adapted for wind dispersal, but could only suggest that the spongy texture of *D. excelsa* seed could serve for wind or water dispersal. Initial seed fall from dehisced follicles in both species is passive and movement in the air appears likely to be the main means of dispersal away from the infructescence.
340:The distribution of seedlings in this study was not solely influenced by the shape of the seed shadow. There is a pattern for the seeds nearest to adults to have a relatively lower chance of successful establishment as seedlings. This pattern was most evident in *D. excelsa* (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*a*) and *T. speciosissima* at Site 1 (Fig. 1 *v*. 5*b*). Hutchings (1986) suggested that there are a number of factors that determine the final spatial distribution of seedlings, including the behaviour of seed predators and herbivores (Janzen 1970) and the distribution of safe sites, while Schupp and Fuentes (1995) warned that the correspondence of distributions or their lack cannot say much about what determines the ultimate distribution of adults. The distribution of safe sites is affected by competitive influences of adult plants (Sarukhan *et al.* 1985; Hutchings 1986; Crawley 1990; Le Maitre and Midgely 1992; Morgan 1995; Tozer and Bradstock 1997) and possibly allelopathy (Muller *et al.* 1968; Crawley 1986, 1990; Hutchings 1986). For *D. excelsa*, the leaves of adults protrude beyond the basal rosette and may reduce light and rainfall at the soil surface within the first 0.5 m of the rosette. For *T. speciosissima*, the lignotubers of adult plants extend beyond the aerial stems and result in reduced soil depth adjacent to the base of plants. Nevertheless, some seedlings were observed growing from the base of *D. excelsa* and from within the area of the lignotuber of *T. speciosissima*, although these seedlings may not persist. It is also apparent that our estimates of the seed shadow of plants did not detect some seeds that successfully germinated and became recruits well away from potential parents. These rarer, long-distance-dispersed seedlings may have greater significance for the species for colonisation of new habitat or recolonisation after adult mortality (Portnoy and Willson 1993). The distribution patterns observed here may change again after further mortality occurs, especially in relation to survival during future fires.
