*Aust. J. Bot.*, 1983, **31**, 293-6

### **Relationship between Time Since the Last Fire and Flowering in** *Telopea speciosissima* **R. Br. and** *Lambertia formosa* **Sm.**

*Graham H. Pyke*

The Australian Museum, 6-8 College St, Sydney, N.S.W., 2000.

#### *Abstract*

For *Telopea speciosissima* the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all appear to peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter. On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground increases with time since the last fire. For *Lambertia formosa* the density of inflorescences appears to reach a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire.

#### **Introduction**

The effects of fire on the Australian flora are many and are increasingly well studied (see Gill *et al.* 1981). There appears, however, to be little quantitative information on the relationships between time since the last fire and flowering of Australian plants (Gill 1981; Specht 1981). Only for *Xanthorrhoea australis* is there a well established relationship (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971; Gill and Ingwersen 1976; Gill 1981): in some places this species flowers only rarely in the absence of fire (Specht *et al.* 1958; Garnet 1971).

The aim of this paper is to analyse spatial and temporal variation in flowering of *Telopea speciosissima* (waratah) and *Lambertia formosa* with respect to time since the last fire. This analysis is possible as a result of studies on the pollination biology of these plants and the foraging ecology of honeyeaters that visit them for nectar (Pyke 1980, 1981*a*, 1981*b*).

#### **Methods**

The data presented were collected between December 1979 and December 1981 in the Brisbane Water National Park (lat. 33°32′22″S., long. 151°16′56″E.; elevation 170 m above sea level) and Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park (lat. 33°36′18″S., long. 151°16′16″E.; elevation 145 m above sea level). In each region, study sites are located in plateau-type, low open-forest (Benson and Fallding 1981) dominated by *Eucalyptus gummifera* (Gaertn.) Hochr., *E. haemastoma* Sm. and *E. oblonga* DC., with a shrub understory composed mainly of *Lambertia formosa* Sm. Both regions are located on plateau tops and hence all study sites have the same aspect. In both regions soils are deep, yellow and earthy (Benson and Fallding 1981) with no apparent differences between the study sites.

The Brisbane Water study site contains two areas in terms of fire history: one area last burnt in December 1976, the other in December 1979. The two areas are separated by a vehicle trail which stopped the more recent fire from spreading further. There are no apparent differences between the two areas in terms of soil or vegetation. The entire Ku-ring-gai Chase study site last burnt in 1965.

Flowering in *Telopea speciosissima* has been recorded in two ways. In the 1976 burn study area in Brisbane Water National Park, the total number of flowering plants was recorded for the spring flowering periods of 1979, 1980 and 1981. For each inflorescence

0067-1924/83/030293$02.00
=== PAGE 2 ===
294 G. H. Pyke

the total number of flowers, height above the ground and number of fruits were also recorded. In each year peak flowering occurred about mid September with high synchrony among plants. In this area and in the other two study areas, permanent circular plots of 20 m radius were established and the numbers of flowering plants within these circles counted every 3 weeks during spring 1981. The numbers of non-flowering plants in each circle were also recorded for spring 1981. Flowering in *Lambertia formosa* was recorded by counting the number of inflorescences in each circle during spring 1981 and in two of the present Brisbane Water circles during spring 1980. During spring 1981, there were four circles in the Brisbane Water area of the 1976 fire, two in the area of the 1979 fire and two in the Ku-ring-gai Chase area.

#### **Results**

#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Successive Years*

In the Brisbane Water area which last burnt in December 1976, the total number of flowering *Telopea* plants has declined dramatically since spring 1979 (Table 1). Since spring

**Table 1. Flowering of** ***Telopea speciosissima*** **in areas of 1976 and 1979 fires during successive years**

| Area | Flowering time | Total No. of flowering plants | Mean No. of flowers per inflorescence | Mean inflorescence ht (cm) | Mean No. of fruit per inflorescence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1976 fire | Spring 1979 | 306 | 79·5±0·9 | 162·4±2·5 | 2·45±0·11 |
| | Spring 1980 | 100 | 64·9±1·4 | 186·0±3·4 | 0·86±0·11 |
| | Spring 1981 | 9 | 62·3±3·0 | 228·8±13·3 | 0·56±0·24 |
| | | Sample size | | | |
| 1979 fire | Spring 1981 | 63 | 171·8±4·2 | 138·7±3·1 | 3·74±0·41 |

1979 there have also been decreases in the average number of flowers per inflorescence and in the average number of fruit per inflorescence and increases in the average inflorescence height. The differences between 1979 and 1980 are all significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test); for 1980 and 1981 only the difference in mean inflorescence height is significant (*P*<0·05, *t*-test). During spring 1981 in the circles in the 1979 fire area (see Table 1), the inflorescence height averaged less than for any of the flowering periods in the 1976 fire area (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) while the numbers of flowers and fruits per inflorescence averaged more (*P*<0·05, *t*-test).

#### *Flowering of* Telopea *in Different Places*

During spring 1981 the density of flowering plants (i.e. number of flowering plants per circle) and the percentage of plants in flower declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 2). The differences in the percentage of flowering are significant between the 1979 and 1976 (or 1965) burn areas (*P*<0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial) but not between the 1965 and 1976 burn areas (*P*>0·05, *t*-test based on Normal approximation to binomial).

#### *Flowering of* Lambertia

During spring 1981 the peak density of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined with increases in the time since an area last burnt (Table 3). The differences between the areas are significantly different (*P*<0·05 for comparisons between 1979 and 1976 burn areas and between 1976 and 1965 burn areas, *t*-test).

For two circles in the 1976 burn area, the peak numbers of *Lambertia* inflorescences declined significantly from spring 1980 to spring 1981 (*P*<0·05, *t*-test) (Table 3).
=== PAGE 3 ===
Fire and Flowering in *Telopea* and *Lambertia* 295

#### **Discussion**

There appear to be strong relationships between flowering and time since the last fire for both *Telopea* and *Lambertia*. In the case of *Telopea*, the percentage (or density) of plants in flower, the average number of flowers per inflorescence and the average number of fruits per inflorescence all peak 2 years after a summer fire and decline thereafter (Tables 1 and 2). On the other hand, the average height of the inflorescences above the ground appears to increase with increases in time since the last fire (Table 1). This undoubtedly reflects the continual growth of the plants, starting from a rhizome, following a fire. The density of *Lambertia* inflorescences reaches a peak 2 or 3 years after a summer fire (Table 3). No information is currently available on either the cause or the adaptive significance of these relationships.

| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | 2 | 23·00 | 105·0±2·0 | 22·0 (*n*=210) |

| Ku-ring-gai Chase (1965 fire) | — | — | — | 5·5 | 3·5 | 2 |
| Brisbane Water (1976 fire) | 195·5 | 17·5 | 2 | 96·5 | 7·8 | 4 |
| Brisbane Water (1979 fire) | — | — | — | 419·0 | 108·0 | 2 |

3	*Aust. J. Bot.*, 1989, **37**, 1-18
4	
5	# **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria**
6	
7	*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*
8	
9	School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.
10	
11	#### *Abstract*
12	
13	Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.
14	
15	### **Introduction**
16	
17	In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.
18	
19	The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km<sup>2</sup> and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.
20	
21	Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km<sup>2</sup>) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km<sup>2</sup>) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia arborescens, Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. Although

For simplicity, scrub of wet sclerophyll species (*Pomaderris, Bedfordia*) has not been distinguished from damp sclerophyll (*Acacia verticillata, Coprosma*).
32	=== PAGE 3 ===
33	Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 3
34	
35	E. obliqua is usually regarded as relatively fire resistant by virtue of its thick bark, it may be rendered susceptible if bark is depleted by repeated burning. Widespread introgression of this species with the thinner-barked E. regnans has resulted in trees with deciduous bark on the trunk and main branches; hence in many of the wetter sites, *E. obliqua* behaves as a fire-sensitive species (Smith 1970; Ashton 1981). Recent fires in the area (1927, 1939 and 1951) have produced a mosaic pattern of regeneration of the eucalypts and could have led to the development of scrub where the fires overlapped within the early non-flowering stage of the eucalypts, or where eucalypt death occurred at a time of meagre storage of capsules in the canopy, such as has occurred at Tidal River at times during the decade 1975-85. Extremely dense regeneration of *A. verticillata* in Lilly Pilly Gully followed the fires of 1951. Four years later this scrub was 2-3 m tall and virtually impenetrable. The ground stratum was almost devoid of
36	
37	**Fig. 2.** The study site spur (L.H.S.) along Lilly Pilly valley looking towards Mt LaTrobe. (a) Dense *Acacia verticillata* in flower October 1967; *(b)* Same site 1986 when the scrub community had degenerated into a hummocky canopy of *Melaleuca, Banksia* and *Kunzea*; (c) Fenced and unfenced plots at commencement of experiment in 1980.
38	
39	cover apart from mosses, sparse *Viola hederacea*, occasional clumps *Goodenia ovata* and rank *Tetrarrhena juncea*. After 10 years *A. verticillata* was mature and 4-5 m tall (Fig. 2a), but after 20 years it had begun to senesce (Fig. 2b). Death of stands commenced on the lower slopes and warmer aspects and by 1979-80 most stands were dead (Fig. 2c). The stems of the degenerating acacias were infested with numerous wood boring beetles, including *Notoceresium elongata* McKeown, *Pentarthrium australe* McKeown and *Menephilus coerulescens* Haag. It is possible that these and other insects have been responsible for the hastened decline of this even-aged generation. In 1978, regeneration from soil-stored seed of *A. verticillata* and *G. ovata* was occurring in open areas between patches of *G. ovata, Pteridium esculentum* and *T. juncea*. 54	
55	On the upper slopes, shrubs of *Kunzea ambigua* had invaded much of the degenerate scrub, whilst on the lower slopes the dominant, root-suckering species of the swamps, *Melaleuca ericifolia*, was invading much of the scrub area. The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare.
56	
57	A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time.
58	
59	#### **Materials and Methods**
60	
61	#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*
62	
63	Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).
64	
65	Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.
66	
67	The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.
68	
69	#### *Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub*
70	
71	An experimental plot 200 m<sup>2</sup> was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.
72	
73	Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

157	
158	#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*
159	
160	The classification of the floristic composition of quadrats (10 by 2 m) produced six groups (Fig. 4a) which could be interpreted in relation to topography. # **Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub Dominated by** *Acacia verticillata* **(L'Hérit.) Willd. at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria**

*David H. Ashton and Jennifer A. Chappill*

School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Parkville, Vic. 3052.

#### *Abstract*

Senescence and death of 30-year-old post-fire *Acacia verticillata* scrub in areas originally supporting sclerophyll eucalypt forest were studied over a 6-year period at Wilsons Promontory, Victoria. The potential for eucalypt regeneration was also examined. On drier sites, *A. verticillata* has been replaced by drought-resistant *Kunzea ambigua* while on wet sites it has been replaced by waterlogging-tolerant *Melaleuca ericifolia.* In mid slopes *A. verticillata* is regenerating from soil seed in gaps in the field layer of *Pteridium esculentum* and *Goodenia ovata* and forming a patchy, uneven-aged stand. The composition of the mid-slope community is determined by the relative resistance of species to browsing and grazing. The failure of eucalypts to reclaim the scrub areas at this critical time has been due to poor seed crops, seed harvesting by ants and intense selective browsing. Exclosure plots have demonstrated the importance of herbivory in modifying this vegetation and indicate potential means of reafforestation without the intervention of fire.

### **Introduction**

In the moist areas of Victoria, large areas of high forest have been converted to scrub of varying height, density and species composition by the fire regimes of the last century (Ashton 1981). Such dramatic changes have been ascribed to the fire sensitivity of the fast growing eucalypt overstorey and its relatively long non-flowering period. Thus, repeated fires at short intervals, even those of low intensity, will kill regeneration before seed has been produced. Alternatively, a similar result will be achieved if severe fires occur at a time of negligible seed storage in the crowns, or if severe drought or intense selective browsing removes or severely damages eucalypt regeneration.

The total area of potential sclerophyll forest on Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) is estimated to be 95 km<sup>2</sup> and includes a wide range of structure from dry to wet sclerophyll forest (Ashton 1981; Gill 1981). Much of the present forest is intermediate between these extremes and conforms to the 'damp sclerophyll' type as described by Opie *et al.* (1984). At Wilsons Promontory (Fig. 1) approximately 14% of the tall forests of *Eucalyptus obliqua* L'Hérit., *E. muelleriana* and *E. regnans*\* have been destroyed in the last 60 years by numerous fires.

Only 2·4% of the forested area currently consists of the tall open forest formation with tall and dense understoreys of shrubs, ferns and tree ferns. Of the forested areas converted to scrub, about 68% (9·0 km<sup>2</sup>) are dominated by *Acacia verticillata* in damp sclerophyll areas and 32% (4·3 km<sup>2</sup>) is dominated by *Pomaderris aspera, Bedfordia arborescens, Olearia argophylla* and *O. phlogopappa* in the wetter areas. On the upper slopes, shrubs of *Kunzea ambigua* had invaded much of the degenerate scrub, whilst on the lower slopes the dominant, root-suckering species of the swamps, *Melaleuca ericifolia*, was invading much of the scrub area. The area chosen for detailed study in 1980, showed both these types of replacement. Eucalypt establishment without the intervention of fire in these communities is extremely rare.

A detailed assessment of the regeneration of the scrub began in 1979 (Chappill 1980) with the aim of predicting the future development of vegetation in these areas. The study site was near Tidal River, adjacent to the Lilly Pilly Gully walking track. The site location and the distribution of vegetation types as determined from aerial photography is indicated in Fig. 3. The study included description of the structure and species composition of the scrub, a field trial examining the possible survival of eucalypt seedlings and a survey of other species regenerating at that time.

#### **Materials and Methods**

#### *Vegetation Structure and Composition*

Floristic composition was assessed in 1983 by gathering data from 78 quadrats (10 by 2 m) along three transects from the edge of the Tidal River swamp to the *K. ambigua*-dominated scrub on the upper slopes of Mt Bishop. The pattern in these data was revealed with the aid of the computer-based hierarchical agglomerative classification program MACINF with presence and absence data (Lance and Williams 1967) and principal coordinates analysis (PCOA) of the data matrix produced by MACINF. The programs were accessed in the CSIRO TAXON package (Ross 1983).

Profiles were drawn in three representative areas to display the structure of the vegetation.

The relative areas occupied by light (<25%), medium (25-75%) and heavy (75-100%) cover classes of the field layer were assessed from intercepts on 16 lines 10 m long on the lower slopes of the degenerate scrub in 1983.

#### *Regeneration of Eucalypts in the Scrub*

An experimental plot 200 m<sup>2</sup> was chosen in a homogeneous area of typical degenerate scrub on the lower slopes (Fig. 3). It was divided into four 10 by 5 m subplots, two of which were fenced with 4 cm wire-mesh netting to a height of 1 m. The fences excluded wallabies and wombats but not possums. Seventy-two seedlings of each of the three eucalypt species which grow nearby, i. e. *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana*\* in the moister areas and *E. baxteri* in the drier areas, were planted in December 1979 in a random block design in three cover classes of vegetation: natural vegetation, vegetation clipped to 15 cm height in a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings and areas completely cleared of vegetation to a radius of 15 cm around the seedlings. At each spot the seedlings were assigned randomly at three points of a triangle, 10 cm apart. This resulted in 12 replications of each treatment and species combination. Seedlings were first measured on 31/12/1979 and the changes in height, growth and survival were recorded at approximately monthly intervals until mid September 1980, and then at approximately yearly intervals until 1986.

Additional plantings were made of *E. obliqua* seedlings 1-1·5 m tall in the dense vegetation surrounding the experimental plots to determine whether larger plants would be better able to establish in the scrub. Seeds of the three eucalypts were sown separately in 10 small microsites of disturbed soil 30 cm in diameter outside the plots, to evaluate the level of predation by insects or mammals on very young stages and the success of germination. All seed was lightly covered by soil, as it had been shown by A. N. Andersen (personal communication) in nearby sites that insect predation by, for example, the ants *Rhytidoponera victoreae* Andre and *Chelaner sculpturatus* Clark. could account for losses of 33-83% of the seed placed on the soil surface within 2 weeks.

33	The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer *(Axis porcinus)* are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.
34	
35	It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata,* *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea, Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

120	#### **Discussion**
121	
122	Purdie and Slatyer (1976) have pointed out that a single model of secondary succession is unlikely to describe adequately a given sere, and this is true for the post-fire scrubs at Wilsons Promontory. The development of sclerophyll open forests is the product of site quality and fire regime (Gill 1975). In the scrub areas the normal post-fire succession has been altered by the removal of the *Eucalyptus* overstorey component in the last 100 years by a regime of frequent, severe fires associated with European settlement (King 1963).

222	In terms of dynamics, the mid and lower slopes represent a relatively stable stage since *A. verticillata* is regenerating; however, much will depend on the growth, toler

225	
226	ance and longevity of other dominants such as *B. marginata,* *C. quadrifida, K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia.* The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny at shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species.
227	
228	The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. With the demise of the *A. verticillata* stratum the high percentage of bare ground was subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The patchy regeneration of *A. verticillata,* which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, *A. verticillata* has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than 15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole topographic range.
229	
230	Only under very rare instances do eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of *Eucalyptus* species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred between the three contending species in the area - *E. obliqua, E. muelleriana* and *E. baxteri.* When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources for *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana* used.
231	
232	In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5 tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in non-fire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant eucalypt seed production.
233	
234	The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance. However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled fire regimes.

the data of all microhabitats because of the low survival in the lighter cover classes. Two-way analyses of variance were performed after logarithmic transformation of each set of measurements. No significant differences between species were observed. However, in 1986 the tallest of the dominant-crowned individuals of *E. muelleriana* (400 cm) far exceeded the tallest *E. obliqua* (256 cm) and *E. baxteri* (285 cm). A longer-term study may show that *E. muelleriana* will come to dominate the site in future years.

The effect of the fencing treatment was significant by April 1980, when all species showed greater height growth (at *P* = 0·05) in the fenced than unfenced plots. Height growth of the eucalypt species in the fenced plots increased markedly in the second and third years, in spite of the severe drought of 1982 (Fig. 8).

The difference in survival between different species of eucalypt during the 6 years of the study were marked. *E. muelleriana* showed consistently higher survival rates than the other species after the first year and *E. obliqua* had the fewest seedlings surviving. After 12 months, only about 20% of the unfenced plants had survived, and after 2 years one plant of *E. muelleriana* remained, and that specimen remained only for an

Graph labels: Percentage Survival of Eucalypts (0-100) against years 1980-1986; Fenced; Unfenced.

**Fig. 9.** Percentage survival of all eucalypts in fenced and unfenced plots 1980-86.

additional few months. The survival of plants in the fenced plots declined steadily to about 20% over the ensuing 3 years. The pooled data for all species in fenced and unfenced plots are shown in Fig. 9. *E. obliqua* was more severely attacked by groups of sawfly larvae than the other species, and *E. muelleriana* maintained large and horizontally displayed juvenile foliage for at least the second growing season.

The fate of large eucalypt seedlings planted at random in thick scrub and ground stratum in the mid-slope area indicated that plants 1-2 m tall could be located, pulled down and severely browsed, most probably by wallabies. After 3 years, all plants had been destroyed, even those in thick regrowth of *M. ericifolia* and *G. ovata.* The last surviving plant, 2 m tall in 1985, had disappeared without trace 1 year later.

Seeds of the three eucalypt species sown outside fences in mid to late autumn, germinated within 2 weeks and reached the 2-leaf stage and heights of 2-8 cm by the following spring. By December, browsing was evident in four out of 21 plants. By the following autumn all plants had disappeared.
=== PAGE 11 ===
Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 11

#### *Regeneration of* A. verticillata *and Other Species in the Scrub*

The development of the ground stratum in response to the exclusion of the larger herbivores from the fenced areas was dramatic (Table 2). The most conspicuous effect in the first 2 years was the increase in cover and height of the scrambling grass, *T. juncea* and the raspwort, *Gonocarpus teucrioides.* Both of these species declined sharply during the drought year of 1982 and only the former recovered its prior vigour (Fig. 10). *P. esculentum* behaved similarly to *T. juncea,* but *G. ovata* declined steadily as its associates increased. The cover repetition of species sensitive to browsing tended to be higher in the fenced plots, although *Coprosma quadrifida* did not conform, due to its development of compact, intricate spiny branches under heavy browsing (Table 2). Species diversity was greater in the fenced plots (26 species) than the unfenced plots (20 species).

In 1986 the increasing cover of eucalypts in the fenced plots appears to have reduced the vigour of the field layer. In the unfenced plots *T. juncea* decreased markedly, probably as a result of wombat grazing. The field layer, therefore, became increasingly dominated by non-grazed *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* and with scattered spiny bushes of *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata.* *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* which are increasing in density in these areas are scarcely browsed, although occasionally killed by wood-boring insects on the lower stems.

The density of natural regeneration of the major woody species in the mid-slope area of the scrub in 1982 and 1983 is shown in Table 3. *M. ericifolia* is regenerating vigorously from root suckers and *A. verticillata* is also regenerating well from soil-stored seed. The later species flowered and set seed abundantly in 1984 and thus further replenishment of the soil seed bank is likely to have occurred in 1985. The reduction of height and density of *A. verticillata* in the presence of browsing was evident in 1986.

The observed germination of soil-stored seed in the field and in seed trays is given in Table 4. The number of seedlings germinating from the seed trays was greatest from the upper 1 cm sample, but the species composition was similar for each depth; therefore, the results were pooled and adjusted to show numbers of germinated seedlings per square metre of soil to a depth of 3 cm. Most species showed greater germination in the trays than in the field, with the exception of *Hydrocotyle hirta* and *V. hederacea.* Some species such as *Bulbine bulbosa, Calystegia marginata* and *Schoenus apogon* appeared in the trays but were not observed in the natural vegetation. The notable absence of *T. juncea,* may be due to heavy grazing preventing normal flowering, since this species is normally present as soil seed in wet forests in central Victoria (Ashwell 1981).

The species subject to grazing and browsing are indicated in Table 5. Scat analysis indicates that black-tailed wallabies and the common wombat are the major herbivores and differ in their relative abundance along the topographic gradient. This will affect the proportion of grazing and browsing in different sites. Brushtail possums were present, and may have been responsible for minor browsing of eucalypt seedlings in 1980 within the fenced plots. Hog deer *(Axis porcinus)* are present in the area but do not appear to be as important as the marsupials at this time.

It is clear that the species which are most successful in the regeneration in this area have means of resistance to grazing pressure. Thus, both *C. quadrifida* and *A. verticillata* are protected to some extent by spines, whilst *G. ovata,* *K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia* appear to be unpalatable to the mammals in the area, although insect attack may occur. In many places it is evident that the greatest amount of damage occurred in the vicinity of animal runs and in more open spaces between the denser vegetation. Dicotyledonous herbs, such as *V. hederacea, Stellaria flaccida* and *G. teucrioides* were severely grazed, but *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* were conspicuously undamaged, although minor insect attack was evident.

#### **Discussion**

Purdie and Slatyer (1976) have pointed out that a single model of secondary succession is unlikely to describe adequately a given sere, and this is true for the post-fire scrubs at Wilsons Promontory. The development of sclerophyll open forests is the product of site quality and fire regime (Gill 1975). In the scrub areas the normal post-fire succession has been altered by the removal of the *Eucalyptus* overstorey component in the last 100 years by a regime of frequent, severe fires associated with European settlement (King 1963).

The early stages of post-fire succession are strongly influenced by the composition of the previous vegetation or by its legacy of soil-stored seed. In this sense the succession is of the 'initial floristic composition' type of Egler (1954). Of the species present in the study area, 13% recover vegetatively from trunk buds, root stock or root suckers and 70% regenerate from seed, most of which is present in the soil seed bank. The relative density of seedlings and root suckers is shown in Table 3. The invasion of the senescent

In terms of dynamics, the mid and lower slopes represent a relatively stable stage since *A. verticillata* is regenerating; however, much will depend on the growth, toler
=== PAGE 17 ===
Secondary Succession in Post-fire Scrub 17

ance and longevity of other dominants such as *B. marginata,* *C. quadrifida, K. ambigua* and *M. ericifolia.* The successfully regenerating species are either unpalatable or spiny at shoot maturity. The importance of the soil seed bank and the ability of species to avoid the sensitive seedling stage by vegetative spread is clearly seen in the potentially dense field and ground strata of this vegetation. In this area the scattered individuals of *A. verticillata* flowered after 5 years, thus restoring to some extent the soil seed bank of this species.

The mid-slope areas show the greatest diversity both structurally and floristically. With the demise of the *A. verticillata* stratum the high percentage of bare ground was subject to the effects of insolation, and regeneration of soil seed commenced. The patchy regeneration of *A. verticillata,* which commenced about 10 years ago, is continuing, but the area available is being diminished as the field layer of *P. esculentum* and *G. ovata* increases in area, density and height. Therefore, at this stage, *A. verticillata* has contracted its range to the mid slopes where the previously dense, even-aged stand is being replaced by a patchy, uneven-aged community, with an age span of more than 15 years. Future cycles of regeneration may further exaggerate this tendency and produce a regeneration mosaic, sens. Watt (1947), although severe fires in the next century may again restore an even-aged community from the soil seed bank over the whole topographic range.

Only under very rare instances do eucalypt seedlings survive without the intervention of fire. The experimental plots demonstrate conclusively the overwhelming importance of the herbivore factor in preventing the regeneration of *Eucalyptus* species under otherwise favourable conditions. Much seed is harvested by insects, and seedlings beyond the two-leaf stage are readily browsed. Over the first few years little discrimination occurred between the three contending species in the area - *E. obliqua, E. muelleriana* and *E. baxteri.* When fenced, the latter two species have survived better in the luxuriant ground stratum, possibly as a consequence of their longer period of horizontally disposed juvenile foliage. However, these data may be biased by the different seed sources for *E. obliqua* and *E. muelleriana* used.

In the event of fire, adequate seed storage in the eucalypt canopy is a prerequisite for regeneration, but even so seed dispersal is likely to be limited to much less than 4-5 tree heights from the source (Ashton 1986). Small areas of scrub, therefore, may be expected to be encroached by eucalypts after fire but this will be a rare event in non-fire periods. Large areas of scrub, therefore, are likely to remain an intractable problem, even if fires of suitable frequency and type occur at times coinciding with abundant eucalypt seed production.

The management of these areas for the ultimate aim of restoration of forest would require the removal or control of the damaging herbivore population, which would be an anathema to the policy of a National Park. The alternative of spot sowing or planting appropriate eucalypt species with fencing guards would provide focal points from which subsequent regeneration may occur under the right conditions of disturbance. However, any measures would be successful only in the long-term because of the magnitude of the area of forest that has been devastated during a century of uncontrolled fire regimes.

28	# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*
29	
30	N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡
31	
32	\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, 0-7050 Leipzig, Germany
33	
34	#### Summary
35	
36	1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.
37	
38	2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.
39	
40	3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1-10 years old.
41	
42	4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.
43	
44	5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (≈ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.
45	
46	6 Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V') decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.
47	
48	7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.
49	
50	8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.
51	
52	*Keywords*: *Banksia*, fire frequency, seed bank model, seed demography, serotiny
53	
54	*Journal of Ecology* (1996) **84**, 9-17
55	
56	#### Introduction
57	
58	Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont et al. 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The
59	
60	Correspondence: Dr Neal Enright, Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, Fax: 61 39344 4972, E-mail: Enright@ariel.ucs.unimelb.edu.au
61	
62	© 1996 British Ecological Society
63	
64	This content downloaded from 209.175.73.10 on Sat, 07 May 2016 01:46:40 UTC
65	All use subject to http://about.jstor.org/terms
66	=== PAGE 3 ===
67	10 Canopy seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana*
68	
69	ecological significance of serotiny seems clear: where conditions for seedling recruitment are best immediately following fire (i.e. competition for light, moisture and nutrients are probably at their minimum), cued release of canopy-stored seeds after fire maximizes the age, and therefore canopy seed store, of the population by the time of the next fire. Any seedlings that establish later during the interfire period have a low probability of survival due to competition with their parents and other established plants (Cowling & Lamont 1987; Lamont & Barker 1988). They will be much younger and, on average, will have a smaller canopy seed bank when fire recurs and so are less fit (*sensu* Stearns 1992).
70	
71	The dynamics of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant age determines the range of fire frequencies for which population maintenance is possible. If fire occurs either before the onset of reproductive maturity, or before a sufficient canopy seed bank has accumulated, then a population is threatened with extinction.
72	
73	In the absence of fire some seeds are released by the spontaneous opening of old fruits, but the likelihood of plant recruitment and survival to reproductive age is extremely low. Seed release is hastened by the death of stem tissue due to drought stress and plant senescence (Witkowski et al. 1991). This means that the canopy seed bank may be completely lost where plant death occurs before the next fire, a fate not shared by most soil seed bank species where seeds may survive for many years after the death of parent plants (Baker 1989). Because dry plant biomass is more readily consumed by fire, any seeds held in the canopy of dead plants at the time of fire are also likely to perish (Lamont & Barker 1988).
74	
75	*Banksia hookeriana* Meissn. (Proteaceae) is a highly serotinous, fire-killed (nonsprouting) woody shrub to 2.5 m high which is restricted to the northern sandplain scrub-heaths of south-western Australia about 250-330 km north of Perth (George 1981; Taylor & Hopper 1988). Seeds are held in a state of enforced dormancy within woody follicles on large infructescences (cones) in the crown. While new inflorescences may be damaged and removed from plants by birds, mature cones normally remain attached to the plant throughout its life. Some seeds abort during development, while others are either released gradually or (especially after fire) are consumed by insects, lose viability and decay, or remain viable. Once released seeds germinate with the onset of winter rains or perish as there is no persistent soil seed bank (Enright & Lamont 1989).
76	
77	The geographical extent (80 × 30 km) of the low nutrient, noncalcareous, sandplain defines the distribution of this species, which is further limited by its specific preference for the deeper sands of low dune crests (Enright & Lamont 1989; Lamont et al. 1989). This means that the species exists as a large number of discrete populations of varying sizes (< 100 to > 10 000 individuals) separated by distances of 0.2 to > 1 km. The largest populations are located near Mt Adams in the northern part of the species range. Land clearance for agriculture, mining and mineral exploration, and increased incidence of anthropogenic ignition, make habitat loss and increased fire frequency potential threats to the long term survival of this species. In addition, its attractive orange inflorescences are harvested in large numbers for the commercial wildflower trade, so reducing seed production in exploited populations (Witkowski et al. 1994).
78	
79	This paper describes seed production and availability, and a computer model of seed bank dynamics in *Banksia hookeriana* in relation to plant age (= time since last fire) for sites near Mt Adams. The following questions were posed:
80	
81	1 What is the pattern of seed production with plant age, and what factors influence the rate of seed accumulation in the crown (e.g. level of serotiny, granivory, seed abortion and longevity)?
82	
83	2 Does the analysis of seed demography reveal the optimum fire frequency to which the species is adapted, and the range of fire frequencies compatible with population survival?
84	
85	#### STUDY AREA
86	
87	The study was located in the Yardanogo Nature Reserve about 330 km north of Perth (29°25′S, 114°58′E). Mean annual rainfall at the two closest climate stations is 513 mm (Eneabba; 55 km to the south) and 471 mm (Dongara; 25 km to the north), respectively. There is a pronounced winter maximum with almost no rain (median 20 mm) in the five summer months from December to April. Temperature regimes are similar for both climate stations: mean maximum temperature in the hottest month (January) is 35.8 °C, mean minimum temperature in the coolest month (July) is 9.2 °C. Soils vary from acidic, leached sands on low dunes to sandy clays in intervening depressions (Hnatiuk & Hopkins 1981). The vegetation of the low dunes is a diverse scrub-heath usually dominated by two *Banksia* species, *Banksia hookeriana* and *Banksia attenuata* R. Br., although up to six banksias may co-occur (Beard 1984; Enright & Lamont 1989).
88	
89	#### Materials and methods
90	
91	Seven sample plots, each 400 m<sup>2</sup> in area and ranging in age since last fire from 1 to 3 and 14-16 years, were established in 1986 and monitored for 6-8 years. They were on the crests and slopes of low, sandy dunes in scrub-heath along the edge of a 2-km section of Mt Adams Road within the Yardanogo Nature Reserve. Sites covering a broader range of *Banksia hookeriana* stand ages could not be located.
92	
93

98	
99	For the five plots where plant age was 1-3 years at the start of the study, and when fire occurred subsequently during the study period (wildfire killed all plants in four of these five plots in 1991), age at time of last fire was estimated for 10 plants by the stem node ageing method described by Lamont (1985), or was known precisely. Seed production was estimated by counting the total number of cones on a random sample of 10 plants and the number of follicles on each of 10 randomly chosen cones per plant. The onset and level of flower head (inflorescence) and cone (infructescence) production were recorded within five replicate 25-m<sup>2</sup> subplots per plot for each year until 1991 (four plots) or 1993 (one plot).
100	
101	For the two plots where plant age was 14-16 years in 1986, the total number of plants and total number of cones per plant was determined. For a random sample of 10 plants per plot, the height and crown diameter, and number of new cones was enumerated each year there-after until 1991 (when wildfire killed all plants in one plot) or 1993. Plots were searched each year for evidence of seedling establishment from spontaneous release of seeds in the absence of fire.
102	
103	Complete cone crops were harvested from 10 randomly chosen 16-year-old plants at the start of the study in 1986. Cones were allocated to annual age classes using the stem node ageing method so that the entire history of reproduction could be determined for each plant. Degree of serotiny was based on the proportion of follicles per cone age class which had opened in the absence of fire (Cowling & Lamont 1985a). Cones were burned and subjected to wet-dry cycles to induce follicle rupture and facilitate seed removal (Cowling & Lamont 1985b). The numbers of follicles, and proportions of firm, aborted, eaten and decayed seeds were determined per plant by cone age. Viability of firm seeds was assessed by germinating batches of 25 seeds per cone age class from each of five plants (replicates) under moist conditions at 15 °C (Cowling et al. 1987).
104	
105	#### STATISTICAL ANALYSES
106	
107	Trends between seed parameters, plant age and cone age were analysed using regression models (SYSTAT 1992). Where data were not normally distributed, logarithmic (ln) and arcsine transformations were employed to satisfy assumptions of the regression models used. All error terms listed are standard errors.
108	
109	A canopy seed bank dynamics model, written in programming language C++, was used to estimate the pattern of viable seed retention on plants and fate of seeds in relation to age. The model used regression equations and other statistics relating patterns of seed accumulation and loss to increasing plant and cone age. Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') and evenness (V') were calculated for the distribution of viable seed ages by plant age.
110	
111	#### Results
112	
113	#### CONE PRODUCTION
114	
115	A few plants produced inflorescences at 3-4 years of age, but these were all sterile (age 3: mean inflorescences per plant = 0.12 ± 0.06; age 4: mean = 0.92 ± 0.23). Plants first produced fertile cones at an age of 5 years. Cone production increased until plants were about 15 years old, after which annual production fluctuated widely about an average of 17 cones per year (Fig. 1a; Table 1). Both within and between year variability in cone production per plant increased with plant age.
116	
117	The total number of cones held in the crown increased continuously with plant age and although the standard error also increased with age, the mean pattern of accumulation showed a consistent trend (Fig. 1b, Table 1).
118	
119	#### SEED PRODUCTION
120	
121	Cones of *Banksia hookeriana* contained up to 20 woody follicles, each of which held two seeds. The maximum possible number of seeds on a plant can

Note: standard errors are calculated for the 10 plants which were aged and harvested at the start of the study in 1986, and subsequently for total cones on random sets of 10 plants each year to 1993.

146	therefore be described by the simple equation: number of potential seeds = (number of cones)(number of follicles)(2). On average, cones contained 12.08 ± 0.04 follicles, with no significant trend in relation to plant age (Fig. 2a). Although each follicle contained two seeds, only 83.0 ± 1.0% of seeds were firm (i.e. had developed embryos). Viability of firm seeds was variable between years (overall mean 74.4 ± 17.8%), but differences were not significant (Fig. 2b).
147	
148	#### SEROTINY, GRANIVORY, DECAY AND SEED STORAGE
149	
150	In the absence of fire nearly all follicles remained closed for the first 5 years. Thereafter the rate of spontaneous seed release increased linearly (Fig. 2c, Table 1). After 10-12 years the cones were heavily weathered and many of the seeds decomposed so that few viable seeds remained.
151	
152	Since plants only began to set viable seed at an age of about 5 years, and little spontaneous follicle rupture occurred in cones less than 5 years old, there was almost no seed loss due to follicle rupture in plants up to 10 years old. Above this age, the percentage seed loss increased markedly: 5% of all follicles on plants were open by age 13 years, 10% by 16 years, and 20% by age 21 years. No seedlings which established in the sample plots as a result of interfire seed release survived for more than one year.
153	
154	The decline in seed storage with cone age was also attributable to seed loss through granivory and decay (Table 1). Loss of seeds through fungal decay followed a similar pattern to that described for spontaneous seed release due to follicle rupture in the absence of fire. Decay was almost absent until cones were 6 years old, after which the proportion of seeds lost increased rapidly.
155	
156	Granivory within closed follicles by the larvae of two weevils, *Cechides amoenus* (Curculionidae; Cleoninae) and *Eleale aulicodes* (Curculionidae; Cleridae), and a jewel beetle (Bupestridae; *Astraeus* sp.) was observed. Unlike follicle opening and decay, granivory was recorded for all cone ages (Table 1).
157	
158	#### THE SEED BANK DYNAMICS MODEL
159	
160	By integrating the information on average patterns of seed production, storage and loss in relation to plant and cone age, it was possible to model the pattern of storage of viable seeds on an average plant of any age, and to identify the quantities of seeds lost to incomplete seed development, senescence, interfire dispersal (spontaneous follicle opening), granivory and decay. The statistical relationships used in the model have been described above and are listed in Table 1, and a flow diagram of the model is shown in Fig. 3.
161	
162	The model first estimated the number of new cones produced per year for each plant age up to 25 years using eqn 1 (Table 1). Number of cones per year was set to 17 once plant age reached 15 years (the average for years 15-21). Estimation was stopped at age 25 years since field data were only available for plants up to 21 years. The number of cones was summed for each possible plant age to produce an estimate of the total number of cones held in the crown at any plant age. The total number of seeds which could be held on the plant, if every follicle on every cone held two seeds, was then determined. Two estimation methods were available and gave almost identical results: one based on mean follicle number per cone for samples
163	
164

168	13 N. J. Enright et al.
169	
170	Figure axes: (a) NO. OF FOLLICLES PER CONE; (b) GERMINATION (%); (c) OPEN FOLLICLES (%); CONE AGE (Y).
171	
172	Fig. 2 (a) The number of follicles per cone (± SE) in relation to cone age, (b) percentage germination of firm seeds extracted from closed follicles on cones of different age, and (c) proportion of follicles per cone which opened spontaneously in the absence of fire in relation to cone age for *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams, Western Australia. Note: error bars are not included for data points where sample size was less than 10 cones, or five replicate batches of seeds, per cone age class.
173	
174	of 10 cones per plant (eqn 2a), and another based on complete follicle counts for all cones on a total of 123 plants (eqn 2b). The latter method of estimation was used in the model.
175	
176	The proportion of seeds lost from cones due to spontaneous follicle rupture in the absence of fire was estimated for each cone age (eqn 3) and multiplied by the estimated number of seeds in that age class. A new total for remaining seeds by plant age was then determined. The total number of seeds remaining was multiplied by the proportion of firm seeds (eqn 4) to eliminate aborted seeds held in closed follicles from future calculations. The proportions of firm seeds lost to granivory and decay were estimated for each cone age class (eqns 5 and 6) and deducted from the seeds available within that age class. Finally, the estimated number of viable seeds remaining on a plant of given age was obtained by multiplying the total firm seeds after losses to granivory and decay by the germination rate for firm seeds.
177	
178	Predicted total seeds produced per plant by age 25 years was 5800. Plants were likely, on average, to hold 100 viable seeds in closed follicles by the time they were 8 years old, 1000 by the time they were 17 years, and 1400 when they were 25 years (Fig. 4). The annual rate of viable seed accumulation in the crown peaked at 15 years. By the time plants were 25 years old, the combined impacts of follicle rupture in the absence of fire, and decay, resulted in little further net accumulation of viable seed in the plant canopy and more seeds were lost than were gained per year (Fig. 4). The overall canopy seed store represented a declining proportion of the total seeds produced, dropping from about one-half at age 8 years to one-quarter at age 25 years.
179	
180	Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages represented in the canopy seed bank increased continuously with plant age following the onset of reproductive maturity; quickly at first as the number of seed ages represented increased on young plants (H' = 0.66 at 6 years, to H' = 2.00 at 15 years), and then more slowly as the number of seed ages represented on the plant stabilised (H' = 2.28 at 25 years). The continued increase in H' after annual seed production had peaked (15 years) and the number of seed ages represented had stabilised (18 years), resulted from increasing evenness (V') of seed abundance in each age class. Evenness was initially high (V' = 0.95 at 6 years), declined as each year's seed crop increased (V' = 0.80 at 17 years), then increased again as seed production stabilised (V' = 0.88 at 25 years).
181	
182	#### Discussion
183	
184	#### SEED DEMOGRAPHY
185	
186	Flowering in *Banksia hookeriana* commenced at an age of 3-4 years, but few or no viable seeds were stored on plants < 5 years old, so that recurrent fire within this time would lead to loss of the species from the community. The time to first reproduction is similar to that described for a number of other serotinous, nonsprouting trees and shrubs in southern and eastern Australian scrub-heaths (Bradstock 1985;

197	
198	Gill & McMahon 1986; Cowling & Lamont 1987; Cowling et al. 1987; Bell et al. 1987). The annual production of cones and seeds increased rapidly between ages 5 and 15 years but then fluctuated

201	
202	Fig. 4 The estimated total number of viable seeds stored in the crown (solid line), and the estimated total number of viable seeds lost to the combination of spontaneous follicle rupture, granivory and decay (broken line) in relation to plant age for *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams, Western Australia (Calculated using the seed bank dynamics model described in the text and Fig. 3).
203	
204	around a mean of 17 cones per year. This early levelling-off of reproduction is in contrast to the continuous increase in seed production with age noted for *Banksia cuneata* to at least 23 years (Lamont et al. 1991b), and for *Banksia ornata* to as much as 38 years (Gill & McMahon 1986).
205	
206	Despite large year to year variations in cone production, on average the total number of cones in the crown showed a steady increase with age. McMaster & Zedler (1981), Lamont et al. (1991a), and others hypothesized that canopy seed storage (serotiny) may dampen annual fluctuations in production, ensuring adequate seed supply following fire. The present results support this contention: seeds produced in years of high seed production were nearly all held on the plant for at least 5 years so that years of low seed production did not impact in the short term on the total canopy seed store.
207	
208	Cowling et al. (1987) found that years of high seed production were associated with low rates of pre-dispersal granivory by insects, implying satiation of granivores. If serotiny dampens fluctuations in seed availability, as suggested above, then these year to year variations would not prove effective in limiting the impacts of insect granivores unless granivory were
209	
210

213	=== PAGE 8 ===
214	15 N. J. Enright et al.
215	
216	restricted to follicles on cones less than one year old. Indeed, Scott (1982) claimed that granivory was concentrated on new cones since the largely host-specific insect larvae which eat Banksia seeds can only tunnel through the soft central axis of the inflorescence. He argued that the increasing woodiness of cones with age rendered those more than 1-year-old less vulnerable to invasion. However, Cowling et al. (1987) concluded that follicle damage from insects occurred in older cones for *Banksia menziesii* and *Banksia prionotes*. A similar finding was obtained here for *Banksia hookeriana* (Table 1): While granivory was greatest in 1-year-old follicles (18%), it continued at a rate of 2-3% of follicles per year in cones of increas ing age. Zammit & Westoby (1988) also recorded granivory in old cones of *Banksia ericifolia* at Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, New South Wales, but suggested that the trend might be explained by higher rates of infestation in the first few years of seed production when fewer inflorescences were available. However, levels of granivory in cones harvested from young stands provided only limited support for this explanation.
217	
218	#### SEED BANK DYNAMICS AND FIRE FREQUENCY
219	
220	According to Gill (1981) plants are not adapted to fire *per se*, but to a particular fire regime. The number of viable seeds stored in the crown of serotinous plants may largely determine the number offspring left after a fire. The balance between the accumulation of viable seeds in the canopy seed bank as plant age increases, and the loss of viable seeds to spontaneous follicle opening, granivory and decay might appropriately describe the optimum life history strategy for a non sprouting species in relation to fire frequency. The canopy seed bank dynamics model estimates these patterns of accumulation and loss.
221	
222	Early in the reproductive life of individuals of *Banksia hookeriana* (5-8 years of age) few viable seeds are produced, but few are lost. The absolute number of seeds available for dispersal following fire is small and there is a low likelihood of successful parent replacement given the high rates of seed and seedling mortality typical of the first few years following fire (Enright & Lamont 1989, 1992a,b). Using data on seedling recruitment after fire in Little Desert National Park, Victoria, Gill & McMahon (1986) estimated that parent replacement in *Banksia ornata* populations was unlikely until plants held ≈ 100 viable seeds in the crown. This correlated with a plant age of about 16 years. Independent evidence on recruitment of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams following experimental fires in 1983 and a wildfire in 1984 indicated that between 45 and 90 seeds were released for each recruit still alive in 1990 at the age of 6 or 7 years (Enright & Lamont 1992b). If it is assumed that 100 seeds are required to ensure parent replacement following fire, then the minimum postfire interval for *Banksia hookeriana* plants would be at least 8 years.
223	
224	The total number of viable seeds lost from the canopy during the interfire period increased rapidly with age for plants > 10 years old. Nevertheless, the excess of total viable seeds produced in the plant's lifetime over total losses peaked at age 15 years. As plants continued to age in the absence of fire, total losses approached and finally exceeded the number of viable seeds still in the crown. This was predicted to occur for the average plant by the age of 22 years.
225	
226	Using the simplifying assumption that self-replace ment, on average, required release of at least 100 viable seeds per parent after fire, an estimate of the finite rate of natural increase (λ) can be calculated for each plant age (= fire frequency) with the maximum value of λ assumed to reflect the optimum strategy (λ as a measure of fitness, sensu Stearns 1992). Populations of *Banksia hookeriana* near Mt Adams appear optimally adapted to recurrent fires every 16-17 years (Fig. 5). Fires at this frequency also maximized the number of viable seeds released after fire relative to the total investment of energy and nutrients expended on seed production. Although the size of the canopy seed bank continued to grow until plants were about 25 years old, predicted λ decreased as plant age increased beyond 17 years. In addition, increasingly more resources are wasted on seeds which perish during the interfire period through spontaneous release into a highly competitive environment where successful recruitment is unlikely, and through pre-dispersal granivory and decay.
227	
228	However, the predicted optimum fire frequency is dependent upon the estimated number of seeds needed to ensure parent replacement. If this estimate is reduced (greater likelihood of recruitment per seed) then the optimum occurs earlier, while if it is increased

239	
240	(less likelihood of recruitment) the optimum occurs later. It is likely that the true value varies from fire to fire, reflecting differences in the suitability of weather conditions for postfire recruitment (Enright & Lamont 1992a,b). For estimates ranging from half (50) to twice (200) the hypothesized number of seeds required per parent (relative to that used above), the optimum fire frequency ranges from 15 to 18 years, respectively (Fig. 5), and so appears quite robust.
241	
242	If stands remain unburned for more than 25 years, opportunities for interfire recruitment might increase due to the release of sites within stands resulting from death of old individuals. However, Bond (1980) documents the decline of serotinous Proteaceae populations in South African fynbos which have remained unburned for 30-65 years, and we have recorded no successful interfire recruitment to reproductive age in *Banksia hookeriana* for stands up to 21 years old. The lack of older sites precludes further direct study of this question. The wastage of scarce resources (i.e. seed loss) in plants older than 22 years might imply that, historically, sites rarely reach this age before fire recurs. In support of this contention, we have been unable to locate any sites containing plants older than 23 years (Enright & Lamont unpublished data). How ever, this may also reflect a recent increase in fire frequency due to human interference.
243	
244	Diversity and evenness in the canopy seed store modelled here had not peaked by the estimated optimum return time for fire. Nevertheless, diversity (H') rises only slowly once this optimum is passed and evenness is always high. One possible consequence of dormant seed banks is the presence of seeds produced in different years which might reflect different pollen parents and selective forces (Harper 1977), i.e. it increases genetic diversity of the seed pool. This might help to buffer the species against rapid evolutionary drift, and at the same time increase resilience of the species in the face of fluctuating environmental conditions. These advantages apply to short-lived species characterized by soil seed storage where parent plants represent different generations. The advantages for longer lived, cohort regenerator species such as *Banksia hookeriana* are less obvious, as all or most pollen will derive from neighbours of identical age which were recruited following the same disturbance and have experienced similar growing conditions. Instead, selfing would probably increase with age as flower head production per plant and death of neighbours increased, cancelling out increasing seed age diversity. Cowling (1987) argued that serotinous nonsprouting species (such as *Banksia hookeriana*) are prone to strong selection pressure, particularly at the seedling stage. He considered that the high number of discrete sexual generations, and fragmentation of populations through fire-mediated local extinction, implies a rapid evolutionary rate and may explain the high level of speciation in Banksia and other taxa with similar life histories.
245	
246	The recent history of fire within the geographical range of *Banksia hookeriana* suggests shorter intervals between successive fires than we propose as optimal for species' maintenance. A wildfire in January 1984 burned 117 000 ha of the northern sandplain heath (van der Moezel et al. 1987), an area equivalent to nearly half of the total geographical range of the species. In the autumn of 1991 wildfire again covered part of the 1984 burn area near Mt Adams, a return period of only 7 years. This fire eliminated *Banksia hookeriana* from one of the plots enumerated here. Van der Moezel et al. (1987) comment that areas of sandplain heath vegetation older than 11 years are becoming increasingly scarce since the establishment of farms and roads in the area and a hazard-reduction burning policy for the remaining natural vegetation.
247	
248	#### Acknowledgements

The authors acknowledge assistance in the field provided by Stephen van Leeuwen, Stephen Bergl and Ed Witkowski in particular, and the many students and research assistants from the School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, Perth, who helped at various times. Insect species were identified by scientific staff of the Western Australian Museum, Perth.

# Canopy seed bank dynamics and optimum fire regime for the highly serotinous shrub, *Banksia hookeriana*

N.J. ENRIGHT,\*† BYRON B. LAMONT† and RALF MARSULA‡

\*Department of Geography and Environmental Studies, University of Melbourne, Parkville, 3052, Australia, †School of Environmental Biology, Curtin University of Technology, GPO Box U1987 Perth, 6001, Australia and ‡Sektion Ökosystemanalyse, UFZ-Umweltforschungszentrum, Leipzig-Halle GmbH, Permoserstr. 15, PF 2, 0-7050 Leipzig, Germany

#### Summary

1 *Banksia hookeriana* is a serotinous nonsprouting shrub restricted to the fire-prone northern sandplain scrub-heaths of Western Australia. Evidence of the natural fire frequency to which the species is best adapted was sought through analysis of its seed demography using a computer model of canopy seed bank dynamics based on field data.

2 Plants began flowering at 3-4 years of age but storage of viable seeds in the canopy was rare for plants < 5 years. Infructescences (cones) contained a mean of 12 follicles, holding two seeds of which 62% were estimated to be viable.

3 Cone (and seed) production increased with plant age to 15 years, but then fluctuated widely around a mean of 17 cones per year. By this time the average plant had an estimated canopy seed bank of 700 viable seeds comprising seeds 1-10 years old.

4 Seeds were lost from the canopy seed bank through spontaneous follicle rupture (i.e. in the absence of fire), granivory by insect larvae, and decay. Most follicles remained closed for at least 5 years and up to 50% of follicles were still closed after 10 years. Insect granivores destroyed 18% of seeds in 1-year-old cones, and continued to destroy seeds in older cones at a rate of 2-3% per year.

5 The seed bank model predicted continued seed accumulation in the canopy to at least age 25 years (1400 seeds), but by this time more viable seeds (≈ 2200) had been lost to spontaneous opening, granivory and decay than were then stored on the plant.

6 Shannon-Weiner diversity (H') of seed ages in the canopy seed bank increased with plant age, while evenness (V') decreased at first (to plant age 17 years) and then increased.

7 On a time-scale of many generations, the likelihood of successful recruitment of individuals in the next generation (on average), occurs for a fire frequency of 15-18 years. At this frequency resource wastage in this low-nutrient environment would be minimized.

8 Recent fires have recurred within 7-11 years and indicate a human impact on the natural fire regime which may ultimately threaten the species.

#### Introduction

Serotiny refers to the retention of seeds in closed fruits within the plant canopy for more than one year, and can be contrasted with two alternative fates of seeds: storage in a soil seed bank, or release of short-lived seeds upon maturity (no seed storage) (Lamont et al. 1991a). Seed release in serotinous species is normally triggered by fire and seeds are short-lived after release, germinating during the first favourable period (Cowling & Lamont 1987). Species can range from weakly serotinous, where most seeds are released within a few years of production, to strongly serotinous, where seeds are held in the canopy for many years. The
